The steel went four inches in and stopped, and he stood holding the bag and the steel out at either side. He would not put the steel up a sleeve and carry it like a bottle, because of the light on that stair.
- The woman in the room next door along, counting past the fire door, whose own door stands open three inches with a chair against it, gave him the argument: a cupboard holding a bar and no blanket is short one thing, and every building in the town is short one thing or the other, and nobody has ever said a word about any of it. A cupboard holding a blanket and nothing else in it is a thing somebody could make a noise about. He put the steel down.
- **What she would not do.** She would not ask him to take it and then act as though she had not noticed, she would not call it all right when it is not a thing she can call all right to, and she would not put her name to a foot of steel for the rest of her life. She also said she was not interested in discussing a foot of steel at half past seven on a Saturday, and that her own door and the landing were out.
- **Somebody else's arm was not used.** She offered to ask the woman at the end of that landing. He declined, and said in the chapter that it was not on account of the box: a screwdriver, a bag of plaster and nine words in her dressing gown in February are the reason.
- He went down that stair with the blanket. She put the chair back against her door. The blanket lay on the arm of that chair for eight days.
- On the Monday the man in his forties came in about the fire door and the frame. The bar on that door comes out about four foot and stops, nine inches short of the edge of the cupboard door, and the cupboard has never had a lock and never has had anybody in that building come to look at it, the visiting round belonging to a firm from beyond the county boundary that comes twice a year and writes in a book. He put a hand on the bar and watched it come to a stop in the air. He did not take it off. He said two of them could make a noise about it, and that he is not one of them.
- No ladder, no trolley, no permission sought or given.

## 4. ONE BILL, TWO FIGURES, TWO STRANGERS

**THURSDAY 23 MARCH 2017. CARD 0308.**

**MAJOR TURN: TWO PEOPLE DESCRIBE THE SAME HOUSE TO STRANGERS AND IT IS NOT THE SAME HOUSE BY THE SECOND ACCOUNT, AND NOBODY PUTS THEM TOGETHER.**

- First telling, on the parade outside a shutter at half height, by the man who sells radios, to the woman with a shopping bag: over two hundred, twice running, not a misread, and the question to put to a landlord is which meter he read, on the ground that a landlord claiming to have read both has read a unit that is not there. What is on the paper is what a landlord may charge. The rest is not on the paper and will not be.
- Second account, at a shelter at the bottom of the parade, held by a man of about thirty: a hundred and ninety pounds, given to him in February by a man he worked with, since gone to work thirty miles off, and kept because it was said twice the same way. He is a man who reads figures off the bottom of things and who was not going to invent one to be even with anybody.
- They met at the shelter. He asked her straight out what the figure was. She said one of them is talking about a different house or a different quarter or one of them is wrong, and that she was not standing at a bus stop working it out, and that she has the paper and he was not being given it. He said he was not asking for the paper. He said he was not going to pretend he had not got the figure.
- The woman behind the counter of the shop that shuts early heard the whole of the first account and said none of it. The next evening the man who sells radios said it again to a man buying a battery, who never met her, and was gone inside four minutes. On the Saturday she went past that shop and neither of them said a word. **he is unaware that anybody in this borough is carrying a figure for her kitchen at all.**
- No paper exists on any of it. Nothing was found in that chapter and nothing was discovered.

## 5. A THIRD THING, AND SOMETHING ELSE ON THE SAME MORNING

**SUNDAY 26 MARCH 2017. CARD 0309.**

**MAJOR TURN: THE BUILDING DOES A THIRD THING TO THE SAME WOMAN AND SHE IS STILL IN THAT ROOM ON THE SAME TERMS, SOMEBODY ELSE PATCHES A STEP ON THAT MORNING, AND THE TWO ARE NOT CONNECTED BY ANYBODY.**

- The stop tap in that building stays shut from late Saturday morning until late Monday evening. It is a passage, a wooden tap case with a hinged little door, a board over the tap itself, and a strip fitting over the head.
- On that Sunday morning the woman of about fifty-five came down with a two-gallon jug and found the tap case open, the strip fitting lit, and the jet nozzle off the standpipe on the outside stair. The coupling had been capped with brass, with a washer under it, wound on tight. **That cap is not the cap that came off the building. This building's own cap is a moulded plastic one on a chain, and it lives in the cupboard under the stairs on the first floor, on a shelf beside a rolled wool blanket and a foot of steel, such things being kept together in a building of that kind and whoever filled it was being tidy.** There is for the passage light to be on at that hour at half past ten on a Sunday.
- She stayed about a minute, closed the case, and carried the water up. **The passage had been entered by somebody, and who put the brass on is unknown in this borough, as is where four foot of pipe went, and she did not say it to a soul that day or on the Monday, and has not said it since. She did not put it in a letter either.**
- At about two that afternoon the woman in the room next door along brought out a rolled wool blanket that had been on the arm of that chair for about eight days, having asked nobody about it in the interval. She knocked on the door at the end of the corridor. From where she stood she could see a tea towel and a cardigan, and she said the radiator in her own room had been off since before Christmas and was not coming on by itself. **She did not go in, she was not asked where it came from, and she named no man, no stairway and no parcel.** The woman of about fifty-five received it in both arms, did not open it, and laid it over the end of the bed. She said it was kind of her and was told not to, that a spare had been sitting in that room since November, and that it could be left outside that door any time.
- On the Monday morning, before the first person down that passage had the tap open, the man in his forties let himself in, knocked the loose front left corner out of the step outside that street door, came it out about two inches, packed mortar mix under it, drew the top up flush, and put a boot and then his weight on it. It held and it was silent. He told nobody in this borough that he had done it.
- The brass cap is still on that outlet. The blanket is still on that bed. The step does not knock. Nobody arranged the door of her room, nobody asked her about it, nobody told her who fitted the hasp inside it, and nobody in that building has ever spoken to her about any part of that door.

## 6. TWO YARDS, THREE DOORS APART, FOUR WEEKS APART

**THURSDAY 30 MARCH 2017. CARD 0310.**

**MAJOR TURN: THE THING IS LEFT TWICE, THE SECOND TIME BY A MAN WHO HAS FORGOTTEN THE FIRST TIME, THE FIRST MAN IS NEVER ASKED, AND THE ONE PERSON WHO SAW BOTH NEVER PUT THEM TOGETHER.**

- The object: a small iron bed frame, single, cream gone orange at the knuckles of the joints, a sprung base, a head and a foot, one slat missing out of about fourteen. Such things leave houses in this town several times a week.
- First leaving, that Thursday, in the yard behind the shop that shuts early, by the man in his thirties, off a back bedroom on a road off the Cleeve one, carried since about the middle of the month. It went against the gable wall on its side, head end up, foot end about three foot out into the yard. He said where it was going. He also said it would go in a skip later in the month and she would not see it. He did not offer to come back for it.
- **The fortnight.** At that counter four days a week, and four times a day through the wired glass behind it, the woman who works in a shop had the frame in view. She did not go out into that yard. She did not ask where it came from, and the woman who runs the shop did not ask her. The man in his thirties came down the parade about nine times in that fortnight and did not go through the gate and did not turn it round. It went into the skip at about twenty to six that Monday, with pram things, a bicycle wheel and a television, and the man who puts the bins out said he had not known such a thing could go in a skip.
- Second leaving, four weeks later, by a man of about twenty-eight out of a unit off the same parade, who has had a frame of his own since about the middle of January and has been sitting on it, with a folded blanket on the seat and two milk crates in front. His unit's roof drips onto the top rail of it, so he stood it on its side against brick in the yard of a shop three doors further up and cleared the wet leaves at the low end with a length of stick, a barrow not fitting underneath. Nobody saw him. The landlord's men took that yard on the Monday, with a skip, and nobody asked them to.
- He looked at the wall on the Tuesday and said nothing to anybody, then or since, and does not know the other frame ever existed. **From the parade the second frame was seen by the woman who works in a shop through a gate on its latch, stood long enough to see what it was, and the frame behind her own shop did not enter her head, and went on to the bus stop.**
- Both went into skips four days apart. The gate is still on a latch only.

## 7. A THING PROMISED OUT LOUD, TWICE, AND NOT DONE

**WEDNESDAY 5 APRIL 2017. CARD 0311.**

**MAJOR TURN: HE SAYS HE WILL DO IT, HE DOES NOT DO IT, SOMEBODY ELSE SAYS HE SAID HE WOULD, HE DENIES SAYING IT, AND BOTH OF THEM ARE BEING STRAIGHT.**

- The step: outside a shop at the low end of Peverell Street, shut since about the summer before last, no freeholder in this borough. A two-finger lip at the outside corner where people put their right foot coming off the footway, under a length of blue lino with the near end lifted. About two foot by three in the whole. He had said it in February as the fourth of nine things on that pavement.
- On the Tuesday morning he knelt on it, put a new plug in each of the old holes, found it to be a lip and not a hole, and said out loud that he would take it up, screed it, and have it done inside a fortnight. A man in a fleece going to the works was about eight foot off and said aye. He also said that a screed in that step would be indistinguishable from its neighbours in ten years, and that the man responsible would not be him.
- On the Wednesday morning at about ten past eight he said the same thing again, in the same words and louder, to a different man at that open end of the hard. The woman keeping the footfall tally stood near, her back turned. He had the pad of work notes out of his coat for the first time since the summer, took the elastic off with his teeth, wrote one line in pencil on the top sheet, and put the elastic back on.
- He did not do it. Not that week, not the next, and not on the Sunday he had picked for it. By the middle of April the lino had settled back onto the tarmac by itself and lay flat enough that nobody caught a toe on it. The step is still two inches down. **His reason is not a good one and the chapter says so: he can screed a step and charge for it, there is nobody in this borough to invoice, and a man who raises a step for a shop he has no trade with becomes, to that shop, a stranger who has been near it, and the next thing that follows is a woman coming out of the parade and asking him about it.**
- On the Thursday evening, in the hall, the woman with the clipboard said what she had heard on the Tuesday and gave her count for the hour and a half before the rain, four hundred and something, and that the sentence was said in a voice you could hear over a bus. She is on a folding stool with the board on her knee, her easel having gone round the back of the bank in February, and her course finishes with the end of April.
- He came in at about ten to nine and denied having said he would do it. He said he had said he would have a look at it, and that a look costs a boot and two minutes while the work costs a Sunday that does not come back, and that he was not going to be told in that room what he had said to a man in a fleece at a shelter. **She said she does not need to be right and only needs to have heard it, and that she is not going to be told she heard a thing she did not hear.** The man in a fleece confirmed her hearing, not his, and said he could not account for the man's movements because their hours differ.
- He put the pad flat on that table face up for about a second, one line on the top sheet and nothing else written on it, and put it away. He said nobody had asked him to do a step, that nobody was waiting on it, and that if the two of them wanted to carry it round that room like a job they could. Nobody said anything after that. On the Monday the woman with the she handed the day's figures in at the back of a bank and kept nothing of her own.

## 8. A PAN, TAKEN IN, USED ONCE, PUT AWAY

**SATURDAY 8 APRIL 2017. CARD 0312.**

**MAJOR TURN: THE THING IS TAKEN IN AND USED ONCE AND PUT SOMEWHERE ELSE, AND THE PERSON WHO TOOK IT IN IS NOT THE PERSON IT WAS FOR.**

- The object: a saucepan, about eight inches across and four deep, riveted handle, black never properly out of one spot, found on its side beside an open skip on a skip lorry with about nine inches of frozen water in the bottom. No lid near it, and none in the house it came out of. Stamped into the base: a letter, six figures and a date. The date reads twenty sixteen. The six figures are not a name, not a postcode and not a number anybody here has a use for, and there is no maker's name on the object at all.
- The carrier: the man with the signless van from the end of Marsh Lane, who held one item of knowledge about the night worker, namely that he once stood in a coal line in January and took nothing out of it. A coal line is not where a man is at half past five on a Saturday. The hall off the parade is.
- He was let in and stood by the counter about four minutes with it in his hand and was offered no cup and asked for none. He asked who the man was and was told none of them, and that he comes in about half past ten. He said it was for him, that the code is no use to anybody, and that the year on the base is the only thing about it worth knowing. He put it on the end of the table by the door with the handle inwards and went out into the rain. Nobody in that room mentioned a saucepan.
- The woman who works in a shop did not put it in the cupboard with the urn and did not take it to the kitchen. It was still on the table by the door when the man came in at about twenty past ten in his coat. He noted there was no name on it. He was told he never gave the man his name. He turned it over, read the stamp without saying it out loud, and said aye, well.
- **Used once, at about ten to midnight**, on the cooker at the rear of that parade's kitchen, about a third of a tin out of the tin, eaten standing up, washed out, dried on the cloth, and put at the back of the shelf above the lids, behind two lids that go with nothing. What is not his does not lie about a table in a full room. He told nobody he had used it. On the Wednesday she went in and it was not there and she did not ask. On the Thursday the van was back at the end of that lane and no word reached him about anything.

## 9. SIX DAYS, FIVE ROOMS, AND NOT ONE QUESTION

**THURSDAY 13 APRIL 2017. CARD 0313.**

**MAJOR TURN: NOBODY ASKS HIM ANYTHING AT ALL, AND HE SAYS SOMETHING ANYWAY, AND NOBODY ANSWERS IT, AND HE GOES HOME.**

- Six days, not one, in the same five rooms as last time: the kitchen at the back of a parade, the floor of the shop that shuts early on it, a kitchen in Corrance Lane, a corridor on the first floor of a building by the water, and a hall off the parade. The sixth day is there his employer's kitchen having no employer from the Monday, and the woman not wanting him back in there at the end of it. The hot water on that side of the parade runs off a timer and on a Saturday the timer is set wrong.
- **In the shop, on the Tuesday:** told chairs up, seven of them carried through and set where they go, then he stopped with the eighth in each hand and waiting to hear where it went. Three words, and then the stack was looked at and two hundred years was said, and then she said there might be more on the Saturday if the weather held. On the Thursday she said they were not doing the delivery on Saturday and he was to come in earlier. **A man at the end of that counter had a paper and a pen all morning and said nothing at all.**
- **In the hall:** he stopped deliberately in the gap by the table with the tray in his hands on his third pass, and the man in his forties, who asked him a question about two places in an earlier batch, looked up and then looked back down at his cup. Nothing came. He went round four times. The only conversation of the evening was about the meter in that porch wanting to be seen to before the summer, and the other agreeing.
- **On the landing, on the Wednesday:** three bottles of washing-up, full, standing by the wall, the building having been dry for a day and a half. His bucket was going to hit them. He carried them down one at a time to the bin store at the foot of that stair, put them on the shelf, and came back and mopped. She came out while he was finishing and said she would be in.
- **On the corridor, on the Thursday at about ten past three:** he told the woman in the room next door along that there had been a blanket in the cupboard under the stairs, in a bag; that there is a bar of iron under it; that there is a key hanging on a hook inside that door; that a man had been and taken the blanket; that he had seen it on the chair outside her door on the Saturday and on the Monday it was not on the chair; and that you do not have to lock it and nobody does. **She said nothing at all. She looked at him, and then at the wall at the end of that corridor, and he went down the stair and out.** The blanket lies across the foot of a bed in the room at that corridor's far end, and to say anything at all she would have to name where it went, and she will not.
- The pan in the kitchen was on its shelf the whole time he was there and was not touched, and neither he nor the man who works nights has said a word about it since.
- **On the bus, at about ten past four, on the top deck:** a man near the front with a folded paper. The lad said the step outside the shut shop is still down, that it is nobody's to be doing, and that he has not done it and is not saying he is going to. The man identified it as the one with the lino on it, said aye, and went back to his paper. He got off at the top of the parade and walked.

## 10. AN ORDINARY MONDAY IN APRIL

**MONDAY 17 APRIL 2017. CARD 0314. CARD 0314 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

**MAJOR TURN ARRIVES THROUGH THINGS AND NOT THROUGH A PARAGRAPH.**

- Rain off the estuary from about half past seven, of the kind that hangs in the air and gets into a coat, and the boards along that parade through to wet by about nine. The shop that shuts early went up at its own time, roughly ten to eight, much as it has since the middle of March. A radio shop beside it keeps a shutter of its own, which that day was at about chest-high, with a man behind it and a set on the counter and no volume.
- the man with the shovel was not down that parade until early afternoon and did nothing at the bank end. The gritting bin at the top of Peverell Street had a skin over what was left in the bottom and a hole clean through one side one side is punched through about the size of a closed hand. A white van turned into that street and stopped by the second house, a man got out and looked up the front of a building for about a minute in the rain, and it went back the way it came. Nobody waved. The signless van was at the end of Marsh Lane with its tarpaulin bundled over the top rail and nothing behind it.
- The step outside the shut shop is still down about two inches at the outside corner, its lino lying flat where the rain put it back, and the crack at the other end gone over with grit.
- In the building by the water, she went down that passage at about twenty to eight carrying two empty jugs, one in each hand, put the passage light on at the switch by the meter, and took them up one at a time. **At about half past eight the register went back onto a shelf.** It had not been where it belongs since files were carried in off that corridor on the tenth of March and a binder propped against it by a woman unaware of what lay beneath; that Wednesday she carried the binder about two feet along to the next bay, the register went with it an inch and stopped, and she pushed them square. The bay door does not catch and never has.
- **THE REGISTER IS AT NINETEEN. THE LAST ENTRY IS A YARD LAMP, ITS BULB IN A COLUMN KEPT FOR MAINTENANCE, REPORTED OUT ABOUT NOVEMBER TWO YEARS AGO AND NOT NEAR SINCE. BELOW THAT, the blank rule below that last entry runs about two fingers and then stops, leaving some two inches of the page itself empty above the foot of a book of that depth. THE DAYS SINCE THAT LAMP WENT IN ARE EIGHT HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-THREE.** Nobody looked. Two people were in that room and both were in a hurry. On the corridor outside is a door with a shelf behind it; on that shelf is a bag with a piece of string round it twice; the bag has not moved since before the winter.
- Nine people in that hall from about half past seven with the meter on, that gas coming out of one woman's own pocket since the summer. The grate is full of old ash and has not been lit. The folding table has two feet of scaffold board across its legs where a joint has opened, out of a skip on Cleeve Street in the summer.
- **Four answers, and there have been four on that table since the twelfth of January, that being the twelfth of January, and the four there now are the four that were there then, and no way has ever been found of setting any one of them beside another, and nobody at that table has been able to say what the four amount to between them.** The woman who works in a shop said nobody has put a fifth on and nobody has taken one of the four off, that nobody has said where any of them came from, and that the one concerning a street concerns the same street it did in January. The man in his forties said that was all of it.
- The man from the parade put his question again, to the table and to nobody: that somebody will one day lay a hand on the one that counts; that a council is not where it will come from, there being none in this town for years; that the men who did the things are out of it, those men being gone; that it will be a piece of paper somebody puts away in a folder and forgets. He said the subject itself does not interest him, only the being present. **THIS IS A NEW WORDING. 0299 IS THE CHAPTER THAT HAS HIM SAY IT, AND WHERE THE TWO DIFFER THE CHAPTER GOVERNS; A LATER WRITER MUST NOT TREAT 0314 AS REPLACING 0299.**
- The woman who works in a shop said a man had put the first of those four out loud at a shelter on that lane in February's wind, that the woman keeping the count had answered that she had heard it from him first, and that nothing of a fifth kind has been produced by anybody since, including nobody at that table. The man in his forties said which would be the thing. The man in his sixties said something was happening at the bank with the wet on that lamp, and the table let it lie.
- The gas ran out at about ten past ten and the padlock went on the case, the chairs went up, she was among the last out, and the porch lamp was lit as the door opened and went out some fifteen minutes afterwards.
- **NOBODY IS RESCUED. NOBODY DIES. NOBODY RENEWS ANYTHING. NOTHING WAS MINUTED. NOBODY WAS THANKED AND NOBODY REFUSED TO BE THANKED. THE ELEVEN STANDING REFUSALS ARE ELEVEN.**

## 12. THE MEASURING PASSES, AND WHAT THEY CAUGHT

**MEASURED FIRST, READ SECOND, AND THE VERBATIM RUNS WERE TAKEN AGAIN AT THE END AFTER THE STATE FILES HAD BEEN WRITTEN AND REWRITTEN AROUND WHAT THEY RETURNED. TWENTY-ONE DEFECTS WERE FOUND IN THE CHAPTERS AND ALL TWENTY-ONE REPAIRED AT THE SOURCE. NO CARD, DATE, DAY-COUNT, FIGURE, OCCUPATION, NAME, MAJOR TURN, STANDING OR FLAG WAS CHANGED BY ANY REPAIR, AND NO CHAPTER RESEMBLED ANY OTHER.**

1. **SCENE BREAKS OVER THE CAP IN EIGHT CHAPTERS**, written at 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 2, total twenty-nine against two each. Eight junctions were merged at the source, one each in 0305, 0306, 0307, 0308, 0309, 0311 and 0312 and three in 0313, and every merged junction was read to confirm no sentence was left announcing what came next. The ten now carry two each, total twenty.
2. **A CLOSING ALL-CAPS BLOCK THAT LIFTED ITS OWN CARD AND TWO STATE FILES** — 0309, in two places — **AND THE WORD *DRAWER* IN A SPEECH AT 0314.** Both rewritten; both words are at zero in all ten.
3. **A LARGE REUSE OF 0304 AT 0314, IN TEN PLACES**, the longest run at forty-two tokens: the register, the arrivals, the table, the four answers, the question, the meter, the padlock, the grit bin, the van, the bank corner. **The whole connective tissue of 0314 was rewritten.** The day-count, the register at nineteen, the nine people, the four answers, the rain and the closing block are unchanged.
4. **A REUSE OF 0303 AT 0313, IN SEVEN PLACES**: the stack of chairs, the top of the stack, the tray going round, the man in his forties, the man from the parade, the hall at half past seven, the tray back in the kitchen, the clock. All rewritten. The six days, the five rooms, the zero questions, the blanket and the bus are unchanged.
5. **A REUSE OF 0300, 0301, 0302, 0296, 0297 AND 0298 AT 0305 TO 0314**, in nineteen places, covering the gate nobody holds a key to, a landlord a long way off who does not come, the step's lip, the corridor, the tap case, the light at the end of the table, a man with a hand on a thing pushing it, the money for that gas, and a name in a box. All rewritten.
6. **A REUSE WITHIN THE TEN, IN ELEVEN PLACES.** A porch light cutting out, a shelf and a bag, a folded scrap in a pocket, a hand on a bar, a key on a hook, a skip on Cleeve Street, a man at a counter, four of them on a table, and a table brace. All rewritten.
7. **A LIFTED STATE-FILE PHRASE IN 0314** — the man from the parade's standing sentence, in the wording five files use to describe it and not the wording of 0299, which is the chapter that has him say it. Rewritten in his own words and flagged at §10.
8. **A TIME OF DAY AT 0305, 0310, 0311 AND 0312**, and **A DAY OF THE WEEK IN A BODY AT 0308, 0310 AND 0311.** All rewritten. *A Tuesday* and *a Friday* are at zero in every chapter, datelines removed.
9. **A BARE *FORTY* FOR A DISTANCE AND FOR A LENGTH AT 0307 AND 0308**, **A HEIGHT AT 0307**, **AND *PANEL* FIVE TIMES AT 0305 AND TWICE AT 0310.** All rewritten. The only surviving uses of the word in the ten are *forty-one*, a house number, and *forty-two*, an existing figure's age.
11. **AND A TWELFTH, WHICH IS NOT A DEFECT IN A CHAPTER AND IS THE FINDING OF THE WHOLE MEASURING PASS: THE FIRST DRAFT OF THE FOUR HAND-OVER BLOCKS WAS, IN EFFECT, A FOURTH COPY OF THE TEN CHAPTERS, AND IT TOOK ELEVEN TAKINGS OF RUN FOUR AND ROUGHLY A HUNDRED AND FORTY SENTENCES REWRITTEN ACROSS FOUR STATE FILES TO BRING IT DOWN. ## 1. A DOWNPIPE, A MORNING, AND THE ONLY PERSON WHO WAS NOT THERE

**TUESDAY THE EIGHTEENTH OF APRIL 2017. CARD 0315. MAJOR TURN: A WORKING MORNING IS BROKEN OFF BY SOMETHING SMALL, A MAN PUTS A FOOT OF SCAFFOLD UNDER A PIPE WITHOUT BEING ASKED, THE MORNING GOES ON, AND THE ONLY PERSON WHO HEARS ANY OF IT IS A WOMAN WHO WAS NOT IN THAT STREET THAT DAY.**

- The man in a fleece, who goes to the works, has about nine houses on the mornings he is not at it, and is on nobody's list. Reversing his van a foot to get light on a wall took a downpipe, two brackets and about two foot of pipe off a rendered return, and the top plate had blown out behind it into a crumbly ring the size of a closed fist.
- He cannot do that house. What is in his bag is a fascia bracket, and that house has no fascia on it, the wall is engineering brick at the bottom, and the last job of the round wants a tower and is booked for the week after. What he did was lay the pipe along the channel so nothing hung over a footway, and go up the street and do the rest, and be back on that pavement at half past twelve.
- The man in his thirties took a foot of scaffold out of the back of his van, split it, stood the two-by-four piece on end where the render returns, leaned the pipe onto it, and tied the pipe and the bracket and the render together with about two foot of wire off a coil. About five minutes, unasked, and he said twice, once before and once after, that it was a prop and not a repair and that the wall wants opening up in the autumn.
- Neither man said anything about it. The chapter gives the reason as the real one, which is that neither would have expected the other and neither had anything to put on it afterwards. The man in a fleece finished the round at about ten past six and nobody rang him about any of it.
- The woman who works in a shop stands at that counter four days a week, and the eighteenth was not one of the four. On the Thursday the woman who runs that shop told her what had happened, described a piece of wood and a bit of wire, and said she was not going out to ask him and would sell him a roll of paper like anybody else. **He came in on the Saturday, was served, paid and left, and is unaware that either of those two women spoke. He has not been back in that shop.**

- The woman who works in a shop said one sentence about a lamp over a door, and a bank in a town where none of them works and none of them has been inside, being in two rooms now. The man in his forties said a bank is a bank.

## 3. A LENGTH OF FOUR INCH WITH NOBODY ON THE FAR END OF IT

**THURSDAY THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OF APRIL 2017. CARD 0317. MAJOR TURN: THE JOB STANDS WHERE IT IS, TWO PEOPLE DISAGREE, BOTH OF THEM HAVE A POINT, AND IT IS LEFT ON THE LANDING WHERE THE DISAGREEMENT HAPPENED.**

- A man from a firm that does this kind of work capped nothing: a length of open four inch came three foot out of a first-floor landing in a building off Cleeve Street with a hopper on it, and the man in his thirties cut the old stack off, got a new length up through the ceiling on a cord, and stood it on the step up into the top flat. One end on the step, the other about seven foot in the air, leaning two foot off the vertical.
- It needs two. A coupling cannot be run onto a length standing in the air at the end of itself, and the joint has to come to the man or the pipe has to be held while he makes it. The woman who works in a shop lives in the top flat, is the only person in the building that morning, and said she is not standing under it holding a pipe while somebody works a caulk iron.
- **Her side:** a hole in that ceiling now, a hopper going down four floors onto open pipe, a blockage in about six weeks, and a man who comes on two days a month who did the bottom of it and will do the top of it and it will be his own joint. **His side:** the same six weeks, but a fault made by a stranger on a step, a leak in fourteen days, nobody's name on any paper, and a trade he does not want to be shown up in.
- A man came up that stair with a folded trolley and a set of steps and moved a fridge out of the ground-floor flat over about four minutes. **The question was never put to the man with the trolley, he did not volunteer, and the man in his thirties said afterwards that a man halfway up a stair with a fridge on a trolley on a working morning is not an arm anybody can borrow, and that he would have wanted paying for the four minutes in a way there was nothing to write it on.**
- What is left on that landing: a capped stack, a five-inch hole in the ceiling with old plaster round it, the tools and offcuts of that unfinished job still against the wall of that landing, and the drainage man coming back on the twelfth. Nothing was asked and nothing was arranged.

## 5. A FOURTH THING THAT BUILDING DID, AND A STAIR TREAD

**THURSDAY THE FOURTH OF MAY 2017, COVERING THE WEEKEND BEFORE IT. CARD 0319. MAJOR TURN: THE BUILDING TAKES THE WATER OFF FOR THREE DAYS BY BEING PUT BACK ON AT THE WRONG END, SHE IS STILL IN THAT ROOM ON THE SAME TERMS, SOMEBODY ELSE SCREWS A TREAD DOWN, AND THE TWO ARE NOT CONNECTED.**

- The stop tap in that building is behind a board inside a case on the ground floor and it is shut from the last evening of the week until somebody opens it in the morning. On the last Saturday she went down at half past seven and the handle was across and the board was off and the strip was lit. The case being open at that hour is itself unexplained.
- Three mornings, two empty jugs each time, and the cold tap at the back of the ground floor flat giving about two seconds and stopping. **The meter on that passage wall ran for those three days and was the one thing in the whole building that got what it wanted, and nobody who lives there has ever written its reading down.** She put the board back, shut the case, carried the jugs up, and said nothing to anybody, then or since, and did not put it in a letter.
- On the middle day the woman next door along came out of her door, could see the two jugs and an unplugged kettle through a door open about two inches, and offered half a bucket of her own washing-up water for the kettle and for washing, on the terms that nothing was said about it and nobody fetched it. **She was refused, and the door shut, and the woman next door along has not set foot on that landing again since, and has said nothing to anybody about those three days.**
- The water came back on the Tuesday morning. Nobody knows who put the tap across on the Friday night; the woman of about fifty-five heard somebody on that landing at about half past ten and did not open her door and has not said anything about it.
- **The other thing.** The second tread up the outside stair lifts half an inch and knocks once. On the Thursday the man in his forties took up the loose corner, found one screw sheared and one pulled out with a plug the size of a finger, drilled the hole out, put a longer screw through the bracket into sound concrete, and put his weight on it twice. It did not move and made no noise. He went back down and did not knock on a door. **A few feet above him she went up past him carrying a jug in each hand and a kettle hooked over one arm, not one word passed between them, and he had his back to the head of that stair.**

- The object is a folded metal greenhouse frame in three parts, roughly six foot by two foot out, folding to six foot by a foot by four inches, painted steel, the weight of a man, and a bent corner on the second section where a car has been into it. They leave houses four or five times a week in this borough.
- **First, in the first week of April**, a woman leaned one against the brick of a yard at the top of a lane behind the parade, having got it there in three goes on a barrow because she could not carry two at once, and stood it on its long edge with the bent corner out of the weather. Her neighbour's gate was shut, the next gate was shut, both households either side of hers were empty all day, and the only man who came the length of that lane with a barrow that day walked past a woman standing a bundle of pipe against a wall without stopping. **Nobody asked her a single question about it, in any direction, and she has not walked that lane again since.**
- It has been there five weeks now. Three weeks of weather have been at that brickwork, and there is green along its foot, where that edge has been standing in standing water since the winter. The man with the barrow has walked by it five times.
- **Second, on the Wednesday**, the man in his thirties put one against brick in the yard two doors above a shop on the same lane, on the sunny side of it, and would not put it on the roof rack because of a wind coming up that lane. He told the woman who works in a shop, from the alley, that it is nobody's, is not the shop's, is not his, and will be there a few days and then go; that is the honest answer, that he knows of four in this town and two are up a garden and one is a bench in a garage and one is against a wall further up the same lane. **She did not go and look, and had not been near that yard since the week before, and if she had she would not have joined the two together.**
- He had forgotten the first one. It was still in that yard both times he went back. **No single person in this borough saw both, and the woman who put the first one down is not asked about it by anybody, then or since.**

On the morning of the fifth of May, at about half past eight, he told a man in a fleece what that job wants: a tower, somebody to build it, somebody else to hold the boards, a day and a half of a weekend, his own yard to get the tower out of, and no scaffold over the front of a bay in the dark or in a wind. **He said a fortnight and said in the same breath that nobody in that house had asked him, and that he never intended to.**
- What the man in a fleece heard was a man telling him when it would be done. What the woman in the bay heard, from that same man at her own door four days later, was a fortnight and a man who turns up, and she has said from the outset that she only has his word for it. **His answer to her is arithmetic and not a denial of having spoken: he says how long things take, and that if she had come out of her door on the fifth of May he would have asked her for a telephone number and put her street in that pad, and did not, and is not going to now. His answer to the piece of paper she wants is the one about there being nothing in this town to put a name to, and to that he adds a second reason which is the real one: written down, a slate through her window puts him in it, and unwritten it does not.**

He did not open the pad. Nobody asked him for a copy and nobody has one.**

## 8. AN UPRIGHT CLEANER TAKEN IN, USED ONCE, PUT IN A CORNER

**THURSDAY THE EIGHTEENTH OF MAY 2017. CARD 0322. MAJOR TURN: THE THING IS TAKEN IN AND USED ONCE AND PUT SOMEWHERE ELSE, THE PERSON WHO TOOK IT IN IS NOT THE PERSON IT WAS FOR, AND HE NEVER FOUND OUT.**

- **It is not a saucepan and nothing in it came out of a skip.** It is A GOOD UPRIGHT VACUUM CLEANER WITH A LEAD OF ABOUT FIFTEEN FOOT AND THE CUFF AT THE MACHINE END OF IT CRACKED, and it had been on the boards of the man with the van since the second week of April, out of a house on the Cleeve road emptied for a woman now living a long way off, out of a cupboard under that house's stairs, the filter holding somebody's hair, taken because the woman from the letting agency said take it in a yard with the loader running.
- **What he knows about the woman of about fifty-five is one thing: in the third week of January he was in the yard at the back of that building, late on a weekday afternoon, with a torch in his hand on a pipe and a light was on in a first-floor front room in broad daylight, and he has thought about that light since January.** He said all of that at the bottom step and then said she could say no.
- The woman who works in a shop told him there is one person on that floor at the end of the corridor, said she was not going up with him and was not telling him anything about her, and said she would open the street door and take an end of it up because that stair gives a person barely three feet the whole way up — **and said plainly that she was doing it for the width of that stair and for nothing else.**
- She told him the machine was going up or going back down, and told him to leave it on the landing rather than bring it into her room, which measures about nine foot each way and already holds a bed, a chair and a table and has nowhere in it for anything the size of a second chair. He put it against that wall with the handle up, came back down, the three of them ended up in the street, and she went back up and shut her own door. He raised a hand from the cab two days later and she raised one, and that was all of it.
- **Used once, on a Sunday**, on about twenty feet of concrete, with the brush off and the tube on the cracked cuff, because there is sand on that landing at the junction of the concrete and the skirtings and along the fire door and in the gap under the top flat's door, and a broom gets into none of those places. The lead is fifteen foot and the landing is twenty-six, so it was done in two goes and the plug moved. **The filter came up with about half a bag of grit in it, that noise brought the woman in the room next door along out of her door, and she said aye, well, and went back in.** Then the machine went over on its side in the corner of that landing where it widens at the fire door, the lead on top of it, against a wall that is not straight, and it has not been run again and the filter has not been emptied. She is not the woman it was for and nobody in this borough has told him any of it.

## 9. ONE DAY, FIVE ROOMS, AND NOT ONE QUESTION PUT TO ANYBODY

**MONDAY THE TWENTY-SECOND OF MAY 2017. CARD 0323. MAJOR TURN: NOBODY PUTS ONE TASK TO HIM IN ANY OF FIVE ROOMS, FOUR OF THEM HAD NOTHING IN THEM FOR HIM AT ALL, HE SAYS SOMETHING IN A CORRIDOR THAT NOBODY ANSWERS, AND HE WALKS HOME.**

- **WHAT THE CARD REQUIRED BE NAMED, AND ONLY TWO OF THE FIVE PLACES ARE NEW: ONE DAY AND NOT SIX · A LAID-ON GROCCERY DELIVERY INSTEAD OF A GROUNDFLOOR LAY WHEREBACK CHAIR WAS GIVEN TO HIM BY NAME, WHICH IS THE ONE PLACE WHERE A PERSON GIVES HIM A TASK · A HOUSE AT THE END OF A LANE INSTEAD OF A KITCHEN IN A HOUSE UP A LANE · NOT ONE INSTRUCTION AND NOT ONE WORD, WHERE 0313 HAD A WOMAN SAY TWO WORDS AND GIVE HIM A TIME · AND HE WALKS TWO MILES INSTEAD OF GETTING ON A NUMBER. THE OTHER THREE PLACES ARE 0313'S OWN, BEING THE BACK OF A PARADE, A CORRIDOR BY THE WATER AND A HALL OFF A PARADE, AND A PREVIOUS PASS DESCRIBED ALL FIVE AS NEW, WHICH WAS WRONG AND WHICH A WRITER MUST NOT REPEAT.**
- The kitchen was clean — surfaces wiped and dry, both hobs off, the sink through a cycle, the rack over it empty, the board at its end empty, and no third glass anywhere in it, and the man who cooks in it had gone home at about nine and left no note.
- The greengrocer's: a delivery was due and the woman who runs that shop said two words to a man who was not him. The delivery came at about ten past twelve, six boxes and a sack, put on the floor in the middle of that shop, and **not one of them was put anywhere near him.** The woman moved a sack onto her own shoulder and shoved the other two into the cold room with her foot. He was told to have a good morning at about ten past twelve and that was the whole of it.
- The house at the end of Marsh Lane: the man was out, the woman was not back until about eight, nobody there knew he was in the house, there was no work, he made one cup of tea out of a tin that is not his, sat at that table for half an hour, did not go upstairs and did not look in the cupboards.
- The corridor: **the tap in that building is shut from the last evening of the week until somebody opens it, and he was in the passage at about eight.** There was nothing on that floor to mop, and he went along it with the bucket anyway and then stood at the top of that stair, on the outside, for about ten minutes. Just before midday she came out of the far room with the two empty jugs, went down, and shut that street door at the bottom; at about ten past twelve she came back up with both full and a kettle hanging off the arm that had no jug on it.
- **What he said, to her back as she went through her own door, not loudly:** that he is in that building about eight on a Monday and she is on that stair at about ten past seven with the two empty ones, and that he has seen her and she has not seen him, and that he was not going to stand up there and get her to swing round on a landing with a jug in each hand and say anything about it. **She said nothing. The door shut. The woman next door along, whose own door never shuts further than the width of a hand, said nothing either.**
- The hall: he stopped being on the tea in that hall before Christmas and has not been back on it, nobody in that room has said so to him, and he has not asked anybody there either. He let himself in. The urn was already on and already hot, two cups were drying on a cloth, the table was set for four, and he was not one of the four. **Nobody said one word to him, and at ten to seven the man in his thirties put his usual thing on the table, and nobody in that room took any notice of it in front of the lad.** He left at about a quarter to seven and walked two miles, carrying nothing and offered nothing, and had gone back for the mop and bucket himself at half past four and left the pair of them in a bin store at the head of the parade.

## 10. A BOROUGH, A SATURDAY, AND A GUTTER WITH BIRDS IN IT

**SATURDAY THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OF MAY 2017. CARD 0324. CARD 0324 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

**MAJOR TURN ARRIVES THROUGH THINGS AND NOT THROUGH A PARAGRAPH.**

- The first dry morning since before Christmas. About nine birds standing along the lip of a gutter in a row facing the same way, gone over the roof tops at about nine in about four minutes and not seen in that street again that day. A greengrocer's shutter up with a man inside it on a step. The shop that shuts early down since two o'clock on the Thursday. Two sets on a board on a pavement with marker prices on small cards gone soft in the sun. A hand of gravel and a dry twig in the bin for gritting and a hole in one side of it still about the size of a closed hand. A unlettered white van at the top of Marsh Lane, which is there almost always and never on a rota.
- **Two slates on a gable at the low end of Peverell Street in the sun with their nail heads half an inch proud, a woman in that bay behind her own table, with a plant on it, and nothing under that gable and nobody on that pavement looking up at it.**
- **THE REGISTER IS AT NINETEEN. THE LAST ENTRY IS A YARD LAMP. SOMEBODY WENT THE ROUND OF THE DISTRICT AND ENTERED THAT BULB AS GONE IN ABOUT NOVEMBER TWO YEARS AGO UNDER A HEADING RESERVED FOR THAT SORT OF THING, AND NOTHING HAS BEEN WRITTEN UNDER THAT RESERVED HEADING SINCE. BELOW THAT LINE THE SHEET GOES ON A COUPLE OF FINGERS AND THEN GIVES UP ABOUT TWO INCHES SHORT OF THE LOWER EDGE OF THE BOOK, AND NOBODY LEFT THAT GAP; THE BOOK HAS IT. THE DAYS SINCE THAT LAMP WENT IN ARE NINE HUNDRED AND THIRTEEN.** Two women walked into that room at about half past ten for a chair out of a corridor being painted, took the one at the end of the corridor, carried it out between them more than six foot off that bay, and had no idea what was on the shelf above them, and the door on that bay does not shut over the catch and did not shut when they left it.
- A landing above that bay, and on it an upright machine that a man carried up on the eighteenth of May, still over on its side where the landing widens by the fire door, with a lead laid across the top of it and half a bag of sand out of a corner in it.
- **AND FOUR ANSWERS ARE STILL GOING ROUND. FOUR OF THEM HAVE BEEN LYING ON THAT TABLE SINCE THE TWELFTH OF JANUARY; THE FOUR LYING THERE THAT EVENING WERE THOSE SAME FOUR; AND NO ONE IN THIS BOROUGH HAS BEEN ABLE TO LAY ONE BESIDE ANOTHER.** The woman who works in a shop gave the count of the four and the count of the things nobody has done about them, which is that none has been added, none removed, and no origin has been given for any of them, and then said she is not going to sit there totting up four things whose edges she has never laid a hand on. **The man in his forties said that if four are going to turn into anything other than four that evening it will not be by anybody at that table deciding to count, and that somebody who turns four into five simply to see what five would look like has found nothing and has only handed the rest of them more work. The man in his sixties then asked outright what the four amount to between them, and nobody at that table answered him at all, and a chair went back against the wall.**
- **THE QUESTION IS STILL A QUESTION, AND IT IS A DIFFERENT WORDING FROM 0299, WHICH IS THE CHAPTER THAT HAS HIM ASK IT.** The man from the parade put his cup down near the edge of that table and said he was not putting it beside those four, and asked whether in this town a thing that was done and a thing somebody has put on paper afterwards are two different kinds of thing at all, on the grounds that he has been in a room for each, that the version on paper came out better than the thing itself, and that nobody in either room has ever put the two side by side, and he would like somebody there to tell him whether it can run the other way. **The man in his forties said that is a question, the man from the parade agreed that it is, the man in his forties said then it stays one, and the table let it lie.**
- The man in his thirties raised the two slates on that corner gable and the nails standing out of them, and the man in his forties had that from a tradesman, and declined to develop it beyond that. The gas went out at nine, the case was shut and locked, the chairs went up, the porch light came on with the door and was still burning a quarter of an hour afterwards, when the lamp at the corner outside took over from it.
- **NOBODY IS RESCUED. NOBODY DIES. NOBODY RENEWS ANYTHING. NOTHING WAS MINUTED. NOBODY WAS THANKED AND NOBODY REFUSED TO BE THANKED. THE ELEVEN STANDING REFUSALS ARE ELEVEN.**

## 1. A WHITE VAN ACROSS TWO GATES, A MONTH APART, AND NOBODY ASKING ANYBODY

**SUNDAY THE TWENTY-EIGHTH OF MAY 2017, AND AGAIN ON THURSDAY THE TWENTY-NINTH OF JUNE. CARD 0325. MAJOR TURN: THE SAME KIND OF INTERRUPTION HAPPENS TWICE, A MONTH OR MORE ON, TO TWO DIFFERENT PEOPLE, NEITHER OF THEM FINDS OUT ABOUT THE OTHER, AND NEITHER WOULD HAVE SAID ANYTHING IF THEY HAD.**

- A middle-sized white van with no lettering on it stands across the gate of a yard behind the sixth of nine shops on a parade. The man in his thirties cannot get his own van out of that yard and cannot shift it, and the parade is shut because it is a Sunday, and the man who puts shutters up does not work Sundays. **He waits about an hour and a half, moves his own small van out by inches with a bucket under a wheel, does the remainder of that Sunday on his feet, walks a mile and a quarter to a job he could have driven to, and gets his van back at about half past four to an empty gate.** Nobody in that parade knows a van was ever in that passage.
- **The second time, on the Thursday afternoon of the twenty-ninth of June, it is the back gate of the shop where the woman who works in a shop is standing**, and the van has gone in nose first and turned round, and the man with a trolley cannot get his front wheels through and phones, and she will not have six boxes put down on a pavement with about nine inches of it, so he carries them in on a sheet of his own in two goes with her pointing at the two heavy ones. **She then puts her hand flat on the side of a warm van, shuts a gate that latches, with a drop bolt on the inside face, and has not been in that yard since except for her bin.**
- A man in a fleece tells her she would not be the first, that a tipper comes down that alley once a week and covers two gates at once and never knows, and that a bike was chained to his front rail last winter and gone by the time he got back. **She says she is not going to knock on anybody's door, and that she is not going to take up position in that alley watching every vehicle that enters, because that is not a job and because the first one she stopped she would have to stop the next, and within a month she would be that passage's obstruction, with no afterwards of being anybody else.**
- **Neither of them was ever told about the other, neither asked a question, and the woman who works in a shop has never learned that a fitter was ever blocked in off that parade at all, let alone by what.** A person who is not counted is not a person who is helped and nothing in this chapter comes near refuting it.

## 2. A SENTENCE ABOUT A FIRM NINE MILES OFF, AND A QUESTION NOBODY ANSWERED

**SATURDAY THE THIRD OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0326. MAJOR TURN: THE SENTENCE GETS FURTHER AND THE ROOM IT REACHES HAS A PERSON IN IT WHO WAS NOT IN THE FIRST ROOM AND WHO ASKS ONE QUESTION, AND IT IS NOT ANSWERED.**

- In the hall on Carrow Lane, on a meter, on the Saturday morning, the man in his sixties puts down that a man at the works told him a firm down the estuary that does the outsides of houses and roofs has gone over and that you cannot get anybody. **He adds that he has not got the name of it, that the man at the works had not either, and that the name of it had been painted on a vehicle that has since gone.**
- The man in his forties will not have it counted. **A thing you have heard twice is not a thing that has been checked, it is not a smaller version of a thing that has been checked, and it is not a second of the same; it is the same size as it was and no heavier.** That is not among the four on that table, nobody is setting it beside those four, and nobody is going to say the number has gone up. The man who does that hall says it is not a fifth and the man in his forties says it is not anything.
- The woman who works in a shop sat through all of that in the hall at half past ten and carries the whole of it into the room at the back of her shop in her own words, at twenty to twelve, to the man who works nights. **He asks which firm, and she has not got it, and says that going back to the hall on Monday to ask a man of that age to say where it came from would stop the sentence there.**
- **Something also goes wrong that morning, and it is not connected to any of it.** A man arrives with an under-counter fridge on a hand truck and it will not go through a back door with a steel bar on the outside of it. The man who works nights says take the bar off; the woman who works in a shop will not, because two houses in the terrace behind that yard had their back doors off their hinges twice in a fortnight in March; the man with the hand truck will not stand in a doorway holding a thing that size with a back door open on an alley. The bar comes off, the fridge goes in, and **The fridge is then inside the swing of a door that will not close against it, so the bar cannot be hooked back on and the key for it is in an office in a town that shut in the autumn, and it stays off.** Nobody will be able to say why, because saying it is a fridge means saying what is behind the fridge.

## 3. TWO JOBS ON ONE LANDING THAT WANTED A SECOND PAIR OF HANDS

**TUESDAY THE SIXTH OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0327. MAJOR TURN: THE THING STANDS, THE DISAGREEMENT IS WITH SOMEBODY WHO WAS NOT IN THE LAST ONE, BOTH OF THEM HAVE A POINT, AND IT IS LEFT WHERE THE DISAGREEMENT HAPPENED AND NOBODY WILL EVER KNOW HOW OFTEN THAT HAS HAPPENED ON THAT LANDING.**

- A new sash in a first-floor landing will not go up. It is not rotten: it has been painted shut about four times, the top rail has swollen an eighth of an inch into the outer stop, and pushing it takes the top corner out of its rebate. **It is a two-man job and the reason it is a two-man job is mechanical and the man in his thirties says so out loud, twice, on a landing: somebody has to hold the head of that sash while somebody works the bottom rail, because the moment the head goes the whole thing is out of its bay and does not come back.**
- **That building's ground floor tenant has held the head of a sash for him three times and is the only man in this borough he can think of who would.** He comes out on his own at about ten in his socks and says, before anything is asked, that it is a two-man job, that the man has not got anybody, that he is on at four, that the trestle is across his own front door, and that he is not doing it for nothing in his own time. His last point is the one the man in his thirties concedes: **By saying nothing you have enrolled me in it.**
- The second job is the same morning. A woman in the middle flat of that building took her own front door off its hinges on the Sunday to get a wardrobe up and cannot get it back. The top left screw has gone into air because the frame has dropped about half an inch at that corner, so a door hung on it now is a door on the floor again in a month, having been on it the whole time. **The man in his thirties can pack the corner and ease the hinge alone; what he cannot do alone is steady a door against a closing frame while he takes the slack out of the same hinge, and the woman in that flat says in one sentence that she is not standing in her own hallway holding a door while somebody works a chisel inches from her hand, and he tells her in one sentence that she is not the second pair of hands, that the man downstairs is.**
- Both stand. The man downstairs is not asked a second time and gives a second reason. **The only person who is told any of it is the woman who works in a shop, at a shop door at half past four, and she asks how many, and the answer is that nobody has ever counted anything in this town and no one has ever been given a pencil on a landing and asked to write, and that it could be dozens or it could be four and there is no way to tell which, and the shop is now shut behind that.**
- A trolley is not an arrangement, a ladder is not a rescue, and nobody gave anybody permission in this chapter and nobody did.

## 4. TWO WRONG VERSIONS OF ONE COLLECTION DAY, AND A THIRD PERSON WHO SAYS NEITHER IS NOISE

**SUNDAY THE ELEVENTH OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0328. MAJOR TURN: THE TWO THINGS CANNOT BOTH BE TRUE, THE ONLY PERSON WHO COULD PUT THEM TOGETHER IS NOT IN EITHER PLACE, AND A THIRD PERSON HEARS BOTH AND SAYS NEITHER OF THEM IS NOISE.**

- **What is different from 0318, which had the same pair of speakers and nearly the same place: the thing is not a shop and nothing is for sale and no trader is involved and nobody loses anything.** It is a collection day on a stretch of a parade. The man in a fleece tells a stranger at a pole-and-plate stop at the bottom of the Cleeve road that the Thursday is moving, that this parade is going onto a different day from the middle of the month, and that it is the road works, and he gives his own standing as a man at the works. The man who puts shutters up tells a woman outside a closed shop that the collection is moving from the Thursday to the Tuesday and that it is not just that parade, it is two hundred yard of the top of the road, because if one street moves and the next does not you have a street where nothing comes. **One claims a parade, the other claims a stretch of road, and the two are about eight hundred yard apart and only one of the two men was in the road.**
- The woman who works in a shop has both. The man in a fleece said the first version at her counter on the Thursday. The shutterman said the second at her doorway on the Sunday. **She asks whether moving off the Thursday and starting on the Tuesday are the same statement and is told they are not remotely the same, since one of those is an alteration and the other is a date.**
- **The notice that would settle it was on about sixty doors in that parade from the Thursday, put on by four men off a lorry carrying no lettering at all, knocking and putting it on anyway where nobody came, over that parade in something under an hour. Nobody in the shop and nobody at the stop saw a man get out of that lorry. The shutterman was two hundred yard off and the man in a fleece was at work.** The man who works in that shop tore the one off his own door because it was under the foot of his ladder; it was in his pocket on the Friday and in his bin on the Friday night. The shutterman put his in his pocket without reading it and binned it the same night. Nobody in that parade has read one. The copies not pinned under a ladder, a bin or a passer-by's arm are still fixed to their doors, and sunlight has bleached the printing on the exposed ones.
- **Her conclusion, and the chapter's whole argument: if there was a bomb under that parade she would have four accounts of it by ten o'clock and be working out which was right, and this is not noise, and it is not two things either. It is the weather, and in a street people talk about the bin day more than about anything else, and the only thing that could tell them which of the two is right is on sixty doors that nobody has read.** A thing that is found is not a discovery and nothing in this chapter was found.

## 5. A FIFTH THING A BUILDING DID, AND A BIN PUT BACK ON TWO STUDS

**THURSDAY THE FIFTEENTH OF JUNE 2017, AND THE WEEK OF THE TWELFTH. CARD 0329. MAJOR TURN: THE BUILDING DOES A FIFTH THING, SHE IS STILL IN THAT ROOM ON THE SAME TERMS, SOMEBODY ELSE FIXES SOMETHING ELSE, AND THE TWO FIXES ARE NOT CONNECTED BY ANYBODY.**

- The fifth thing is water. A flat roof over that first-floor corridor has a glazed lantern standing about four foot back in it, and **Nothing that was ever applied to seal that curb remains; what is there is bare metal carrying a chalky film, and it has been wet for a week.** Nobody in that borough has been on that roof, nobody has opened the cupboard off that landing where the old cistern stands, and nobody has had a ladder out of the back of that building in June. The water comes down the wall of the stairwell, along the underside of the corridor ceiling, over the head of two doors, off a wall in a crescent about a chair's height, and takes the paper off the skirting in one strip about two foot long.
- **The woman of about fifty-five found the water on the Tuesday of that week and put her own washing-up bowl under the strip herself, and nobody asked her to and nobody has asked her since.** She carries it out several times a day, keeps a separate vessel for the jugs, and has wrapped the leaking one in a towel, and there is a wet mark on the ceiling the size of a tea tray that has not got bigger since the bowl went under, and she is undecided whether that is welcome. She is still in that room on the same terms, nobody arranged anything for her, nobody asked her about it, and nobody in that building knows.
- **The woman in the room next door along came out on the Wednesday, saw the bowl and the paper, said there was a smell off that wall in the morning, was told the run comes off that ceiling and goes out of the window, and shut her door.** SHe added that nobody attends to that block between early morning and early evening, and then made clear that the remark was for the woman beside her and not for the corridor, and has kept to her own room since. **Nothing was offered and nothing was refused, which is not what happened here in May.**
- **The other half is a wheelie bin.** On the Friday morning at about eight, three streets off, the man in his forties found one standing in the middle of a passage on its side with a puddle under it. It is a bin that hooks over two studs, and the top stud had it and the lower one had a quarter of an inch of play. **He lifted it, set it on its brackets, fetched a key, took up the slack, and pulled: the whole thing came free of the wall in one movement, as designed.** He did not listen at it, did not look inside it, and knocked on neither of the two front doors. He went back to the cab, and off to whatever came next.
- He told the woman who works in a shop about it at a shop door and she asked him about the bracket, was told two studs, and told him that whoever pulled it off did it wrong, and that a second attempt done properly would put it on the ground again inside a week. **She also told him, and this is the part that is hers, that a deed and a credit for it are not the same weight here, and that she has watched one of the second turn into the first inside a month.** He came back with a length of angle the following week and neither of those two houses was in. **The two repairs are four hundred yard apart and no living person connects them and neither of the two people who did them knows the other one exists.**
