**WEDNESDAY THE TWENTY-FIRST OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0330. MAJOR TURN: THE THING IS LEFT THREE TIMES, THE PEOPLE WHO LEFT IT DO NOT KNOW OF EACH OTHER, THE ONLY PERSON WHO KNOWS ANYTHING IS SOMEBODY WHO WAS NOT THERE FOR ANY OF IT, AND BY THE TIME ANYBODY WOULD ASK, THE LAST ONE HAS BEEN TAKEN AWAY BY SOMEBODY WHO WAS NOT ASKED EITHER.**

- The object is a painted timber gate, four foot by three, painted white, with two ledges and a diagonal, sold shipped in a polythene sleeve with brown tape at its waist. **The sleeve gives no clue at all to its age, and there is nothing in this borough that could tell you whose it is while it is wrapped.**
- **First, in the third week of May**, standing against the brick of a yard near the top of that lane; he saw it from the lane on a Monday because he had to walk past that gate to reach a side gate, and it was there again on the Thursday and the Friday after. **Second, in the first week of June**, higher up the same lane, in a yard that takes the afternoon; he came across it while standing in the middle of that yard for about ten minutes over a fitting that needed nothing, and he told the woman who works in a shop about it in four sentences from the alley and she did not go and look. **Third, on Monday the nineteenth of June**, in the yard beside the car park, noticed at about four in the afternoon while walking up from there.
- **He counted them on the Wednesday morning by walking the whole lane, and the number is three, and it is the first time he has ever said a number about anything like it out loud to anybody.** The third is gone: a wet rectangle on the brick, a scuff of white about a foot above it, and a scrap of polythene the size of a handkerchief on the kerbstone. The first is gone: a standing puddle at the foot of a gable wall, unchanged since the winter, and a damp mark the width of his two hands. **The second is still there, gone a dirty grey on the wall side, the polythene brittle and come away in a strip.**
- He got the pad out in the van and shut it again, and gave the reason: **a pad carrying a number has no home in this borough, a sheet in a van listing three items is a sheet that will be mislaid, and a man cannot know on a Wednesday morning in a lane where that sheet has ended up.**
- **The only person in this borough who watched one of them go is the woman who works in a shop, from her own window, at about six in the morning on the Tuesday.** She was up because she has been up since half past four, the blind stays up, and she saw a man with a barrow go up that lane with a white thing on it and the brown tape showing in the middle, and come back down about ten minutes later with an empty barrow. She did not go out, did not say a word to him, and does not know his name. **The man in his thirties found out about that on the Wednesday, after he had already counted three, and did not ask her to say that she had told him, and she did not say it, because if she says it she becomes a woman watching a lane.** He corrected her once and she was right: a scrap of wrapper on a kerb is not a gate, and anybody who said it was would be talking about the wrong thing.

## 7. A PROMISE HE DOES NOT DENY MAKING

**SUNDAY THE TWENTY-FIFTH OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0331. MAJOR TURN: HE SAYS HE WILL DO IT AND HE DOES NOT DO IT AND SOMEBODY ELSE SAYS HE SAID HE WOULD, AND HE DOES NOT DENY SAYING IT, AND ALL THREE OF THEM ARE BEING STRAIGHT.**

- **WHAT IS DIFFERENT FROM 0311 AND FROM 0321, WHICH THE CARD REQUIRED BE NAMED, AND THE THREE OF THEM NOW STAND APART: in 0311 and in 0321 he denied having said he would, and here he does not deny it and says so first, unasked, and the whole engine is a man admitting a promise instead of escaping one.** In 0311 it was a step and a tally and a hall and a line in a pad on a table; in 0321 it was two slates and a fortnight said to a man in a road and a request for a piece of paper, refused twice; here it is a gap in a boundary fence and a promise made to a man in a fleece on a doorstep, and the third person is a woman on a street counting street furniture, and there is no shop in the chapter and no room and no tally and no count handed in anywhere.
- The thing is three lengths of close-board lying against the brick of a yard, out of a job, never installed. The opening they came from is shoulder height and about four foot across, and about nine people went through it between about ten and half past twelve that morning. **The fence has two posts in it that have been there since about the middle of the last decade, and the lower rail has rotted through for three or four years, and the right-hand footing is cracked, and the job wants a post out of the ground, a hole, a second pair of hands to hold it plumb, a day off, and a man in a yard.**
- **What he said, on the Friday before, at a door, to the man in the fleece, who was up on the step: that he would close that opening before the month is out.** Nine days later he stands in the road and works out in about four seconds what was wrong with the sentence, and the chapter gives it: **The mistake was made off the doorstep rather than in the yard, and a promise made about another person's ground is a promise about their ground, and the man on the doorstep is was never going to be a neighbour to it.**
- **The woman with a clipboard has that gate written on her sheet twice with two different numbers on it, from a man and from a woman, and she knows it is one gate, and the man in a fleece told her at a shelter at the top end that a man had said he would have it closed before the end of the month.** She does not say he did it. She says a man said he did. **He says: I said it, at that door, on the Friday, and he is not going to retreat into a different version now, because he did not, and because and the man in the fleece has put her account to her first, so he cannot arrive afterwards with a different one.**
- She asks whether he will do it. **He says no, and he rules out the two easy reasons first — not the rain, and not that he cannot be bothered — and gives the real one, and then says the thing that puts it out of reach of being a conversation: no third party exists who could have heard it, him and a man in a fleece, and that man is not here.** She writes about a quarter of an inch on the edge of her sheet, looks at it, and rubs it out with a thumb, and does not say that she did that either. She says there is not a column for this and she is not starting one on a Sunday morning in June for a man who told her straight, and that it is a thing that happened to her and not a thing about that street.
- **The pad comes out of the box in the road and is shut again, and what he gives is the other reason: a line of that street in that pad would be the only record in the borough of a promise about a boundary, and it would live in a van.** On the second of July the three lengths are still against that wall and the gap is still four foot wide. A list is not a document, there is no form in this borough, and nobody in this chapter was given a title, a grade, a chair, a seat, a membership, a row or any way of being thanked.

## 8. A CARPET TAKEN IN AND USED ONCE, AND A CHEST HELD OUT AND REFUSED

**FRIDAY THE THIRTIETH OF JUNE 2017. CARD 0332. MAJOR TURN: ONE THING IS TAKEN IN AND USED ONCE AND PUT SOMEWHERE ELSE, A SECOND THING IS HELD OUT IN FRONT OF THE SAME DOOR AND REFUSED, THE PERSON WHO REFUSES IT DOES NOT EXPLAIN AND IS NOT ASKED, AND THE PERSON WHO BROUGHT THE FIRST ONE NEVER HEARD ABOUT EITHER.**

- **What is different from 0322, which is the chapter this one sits against: the object is a carpet and not a machine, it is laid and not run, it goes into a room and not onto a landing, it is stood up against a wall and not left in a corner, the second thing is brought by the same man in the same month, and the chapter's weight is on the refusal, which 0322 did not have at all.**
- The carpet is off a roll, about nine foot by six, a wool one, dark, with a pattern about four inches apart, its backing still fixed to its face in staples, and two people would struggle to lift it between them. It came out of a front room on the Cleeve road in May. **He carried it up that outside stair in the second week of June with the woman of about fifty-five taking the lead end on a count of three, because it is a single and a half with a short bit and a long bit in the same piece and it goes round the corner at the fire door.**
- **She told him, before it came up, that no carpet was going in that room, and no carpet went in that room; what she put down on the floor there was three weeks of somebody else's carpet, and she took it up again herself.** She laid it herself two days later, staples in, and it took five weeks of sand off nine foot of bare boards in one go. **On the twenty-third of June she got a corner pried a corner loose with her nails, wanting to reach the dust beneath, and it was deformed by being lifted and no longer fitted, and on the morning of the thirtieth she took it in hand once more and stood it edgeways where the wall takes the light.** It is on its side now, pattern into the room, underlay to the carpet, a foot across the edge and reaching most of the way to the ceiling that wall. **a floor covering in that room would push every other thing against the walls, and she will not arrange her life around a gift of that kind.**
- **The same man came up that stair on the thirtieth with a chest.** About two foot by a foot by a foot, light wood, never painted, a hinged top and a small clasp on its face, out of a front room on the Cleeve road on the Monday of that week when a bathroom suite was changed about. He got it up alone, put it on the step outside her door, and knocked twice. **He said the whole of what he had come to say and then said she could say no, and that if she said no he would take it back down and shut the door and that would be the end of it.** She said no. He accepted it, carried the box back down, secured the door at the bottom, and stowed it in the back of his van under a folding stool and two trestles. **Four seconds passed between her no and him turning round, nothing was said in them by either person, and neither has said a word about it to anybody since. He did not ask.**
- **THE MACHINE IS NOT IN THAT CHAPTER AND NOTHING IN THAT CHAPTER SAYS IT WENT ANYWHERE. AN EARLIER EDITION OF THIS BLOCK HAD IT GOING DOWN THAT STAIR ON THE THIRTIETH OF JUNE INSIDE THE MAN WITH A VAN'S OWN VAN, AND THAT IS A FINDING AGAINST THIS BLOCK AND NOT A CORRECTION OF THE CHAPTER: 0332 IS A CARPET, A CHEST AND A REFUSAL, THE CARD FOR IT SAID THE SECOND THING MAY NOT BE A VACUUM CLEANER, AND THE WORD APPEARS NOWHERE IN THAT CHAPTER. THE LAST THING THE PAGE SAYS ABOUT THE MACHINE IS 0329, WHERE IT IS STILL LYING OVER ON ITS SIDE IN THE CORNER, AND ITS PRESENT STATE IS: A good upright with a fifteen-foot lead and a cracked cuff at the machine end, taken up an outside stair in May and left on a first-floor landing, run once along twenty feet of concrete by a woman it was not for, and lying over on its side ever since in the corner where that landing widens by the fire door, against a wall that is not straight, its lead dropped across the machine, and the filter still holding roughly half a bag of grit off that same landing, and nobody has run it since and nobody has emptied it, AND IT STANDS ABOUT FIVE FOOT OFF THE BOWL, AND THE MACHINE AND THE BOWL SHARE A LANDING WITHOUT ANYBODY ON THAT LANDING EVER HAVING PUT THE TWO OF THEM IN THE SAME SENTENCE. THAT IS THE WHOLE OF WHAT IS KNOWN AND IT IS UNRESOLVED.**
- The woman who works in a shop was on the front of that shop at about half past four on the thirtieth and he took a length of pipe off a shelf. **He gives the rule and gives the reason: a refusal given at once is a refusal, and a refusal given after thought invites a question is about a second, and a person who stood there a minute and then said no would want to know why, and you do not obtain the reason, and a man who stands on that step a minute is a man who would have put a question to her on her own threshold about her refusal.** He has done that every time he has ever withdrawn from a doorstep anywhere in this borough. **A gift that is not refused is not a purchase, being let in is not a rescue and being turned away is not a falling-out, and none of those sentences is said out loud as a label anywhere in this chapter.**

## 9. ONE DAY, FOUR ROOMS WITH SOMEBODY IN THEM, AND SOMETHING SAID ALOUD

**MONDAY THE THIRD OF JULY 2017. CARD 0333. MAJOR TURN: NOBODY ASKS HIM ANYTHING AT ALL, HE SAYS SOMETHING ANYWAY IN FRONT OF OTHER PEOPLE, NOBODY ANSWERS IT, AND HE GOES HOME.**

- **WHAT IS DIFFERENT FROM 0313 AND FROM 0323, WHICH THE CARD REQUIRED BE NAMED, AND THE DIFFERENCES ARE THE CHAPTER'S SUBJECT: 0313 was six days and a number, and 0323 was one day with four of the five rooms empty of people; here it is one day and FOUR OF THE FIVE ROOMS HAVE A PERSON IN THEM, and he is not asked anything in any of them, and he carries nothing into any of them, and what he says is not said to a back.** It is said, across a table, not quietly, to a woman who is standing still and can hear, with two other people in the room who can also hear. **And the device §11 OF THE 0013 OPEN-THREADS BLOCK CALLED SPENT IS RUN A SEVENTH TIME BECAUSE THE CARD FOR THIS CHAPTER ASKED FOR IT BY NAME; THAT IS A FLAG AND NOT A CLOSURE, AND IT IS CARRIED FORWARD UNRESOLVED AT §11 OF THE 0014 OPEN-THREADS BLOCK.**
- The kitchen at the back of that parade has the man who cooks in it at the far end of the bench, cup in hand, the radio on quietly on low, and three items waiting rather than two. **Nobody hands him anything, no destination is given to him, he knows, and at ten past eight the man puts his own cup in that sink and goes to work with the cloth still in the lad's hand.**
- The greengrocer's: a man brings a sack of leeks in at twenty to twelve, sets it on the counter, says to the middle of the room that they are for the shop and going on the account, and goes out. **The sack stands where he put it for two hours. Nobody asked anybody to shift it. it is light, and the counter runs to about twelve foot with room left over at one end, and the sack stands where nobody's path crosses it, that shop's traffic using the centre line.** The woman came off the telephone, carried it into the cold room herself, and said two words to a man who was not him.
- The house at the end of Marsh Lane: he is in it, in a front room with a newspaper, the two of them say good morning and that is the whole of it, one cup is washed and hung on its own nail again, and at about four it is rinsed a second time and rehung.
- The corridor by the water: the stop tap has been put on by somebody who came down before him and went back up and said nothing, which is the arrangement in that building. **There has been nothing on that floor to mop since before Christmas. He goes the length of his mop regardless.** The woman of about fifty-five goes down at about a quarter to ten with two empty jugs and comes back at ten past ten with both full and a kettle over her other arm. **He does not speak to her this time, and the reason is given plainly: he put a remark to her back in May, got no reply, the whole business stayed with him for a fortnight afterwards, and he had no intention of repeating it.**
- The hall off that parade: the woman of about forty-two holds that key, the urn had been on, two cups were drying, the table was set for four persons, and it offered him nothing without anyone informing him of that. **What he says, at ten to seven, out loud, and what it is about: that the neighbour in that same waterfront block has not been seen in that corridor since a Wednesday three weeks ago, that she goes past that bowl twice a day, that she is the only other occupant of that landing, and that for seven months the pair have exchanged nothing whatever, and he has been there the whole time and cannot tell whether they are not speaking or never were.** Nobody answers. The woman with the key says it is an unusual quantity of attention to have paid to two neighbours, the man in his forties says it is, and that closes it.
- **The thing he says is not about a machine, a jug, a stair, a blanket or a step, and the woman in the room next door along is not in the room he says it in, and the fire blanket was not mentioned to her.** He is on the sink, he has no title, grade, department, chair, seat, membership, row or written sheet, being asked is not a standing, being useful is not a job and being in a room is not being a member, and the question he asked on the fourth of June 2016 was not put to anybody in that room and was not answered by anybody in it. **His bucket and mop were still in that store at half past four when he came back for them, and no resident of that building ever enters that store.**
- The name of the question he asked on the fourth of June is not given here and is not to be given here.

## 10. A BOROUGH, A SATURDAY IN JULY, AND NINE PEOPLE IN A ROOM

**SATURDAY THE EIGHTH OF JULY 2017. CARD 0334. CARD 0334 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

**MAJOR TURN ARRIVES THROUGH THINGS AND NOT THROUGH A PARAGRAPH, AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF 0324'S SHAPE: 0324 WENT OUT AND WALKED THE BOROUGH AND THEN CAME IN, AND THIS ONE STAYS IN AND THE BOROUGH COMES PAST THE WINDOW.**

- the warmest day of that year to date. The tar outside the hall is giving underfoot by early afternoon. A man is on a ladder at the shutter at the far end of that parade at about a quarter to nine **on his own**, comes down, folds the ladder, carries it twenty yard and puts it up again at the next one, and nobody helps him and he asks nobody. A van stops outside the fish shop at ten past nine with no lettering on either side and nothing visible in the back, stands about ten minutes and goes and does not come back. **A man goes towards the foot of that street, load over one shoulder at about half past nine and comes back down it at about a quarter to ten without it, while nine people indoors never once turned to the glass.** A shower comes over the roofs from the west at about ten, goes through, and the tar goes from soft to hard in about four minutes.
- **The register is at nineteen, the last of the nineteen is a lamp that somebody entered as gone in about November two years ago under a heading kept over for that sort of thing, nothing has been written under that heading since, the page runs on a hand's width and then gives up about two inches short of the foot of the book, and nobody left that gap.** It is on the second shelf up in a bay off a first-floor corridor in the building by the water, on a door that does not shut over its catch.
- **THE DAYS SINCE THAT LAMP WENT IN ARE NINE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-FIVE, AND THE LINE IS STILL BLANK. THAT IS THE ONE DAY-COUNT IN THE PROSE OF THESE TEN CHAPTERS AND IT IS AT 0334, ON ITS OWN DATE, IN THE BODY, AND IT IS NOT IN THE CLOSING BLOCK.**
- **The woman of about fifty-five gives the figure, in her own mouth, unasked, unprompted, both hands about her cup, and nobody in that room asks her how long she has been counting and nobody asks her to stop.** She says she counted it herself off a calendar and counted it twice, and that she goes past that bay about twice a day. The man in his forties says nobody's going to check that, and she says she is not asking anybody to. The man in his sixties says it is a lamp.
- **The figure is four, has stood at four since the twelfth of January, and those same four were the ones discussed that evening, no one of them has altered, and the means of comparing them does not exist.** The woman who works in a shop gives the count and the count of the things nobody has done about them. **The man in his forties says it will not be by anybody at that table counting, that recasting four as five to see any attempt to render the count as five yields nothing and only increases the labour of everybody at that table, and that this is not a rule and it is not on anything.** The man from the parade says it has been said in that room before, and the man in his forties says will be said again.
- **The question is still a question, and its wording is different again from 0299 and from 0324: it is the same three-line shape with none of the same three lines in it, and that was arranged on purpose, because 0324's version of that shape is still on the page and a chapter that repeats a shape has to repeat it in different words.** The asker is the man in a fleece, **who has not been in that room before in this account**, and he sets his cup nearer the front edge than anybody else has all evening, and he asks, once, whether anybody in that room has ever been asked to do a thing for nothing and turned it down. **It goes nowhere. The man in his forties answers it by laying his hands flat down and saying that the thing is a question and is going to remain one, and the man in a fleece accepts that, and nobody at that table carried it further.** Two matters stand exactly where they stood in May and neither of them is developed: the two slates are still on that corner gable and their nail heads have come further out of them since the spring, and the man in his forties will not take a tradesman's word further than a tradesman's word. **AND THE ROOM EMPTIES DIFFERENTLY FROM THE WAY IT EMPTIED IN MAY, WHICH IS THE OTHER HALF OF WHAT IS NEW IN THIS CHAPTER: nothing goes out at nine, the case is shut and locked about twenty minutes later, the chairs go up one at a time by whoever is nearest and the hall man takes the last two without asking, the corner lamp outside comes on of its own accord and burns until half past six in the morning, and a light on the door side was on throughout and neither the man who does that hall nor anybody else in that room can say which of the two lamps he turned on.**
- **There are nine of them in that room and the room will hold nine. Eight of them were in that room in late May, and any one of those eight could be named in about a minute by anybody sitting there, and nobody in that room has ever named them or written them down. They are the hall man, who is on his feet all evening; the man in his forties, who has the place by the door; the man in his sixties, who has the seat with the split in it; the man in his thirties, who came in late; the man who works nights, who is standing up in his coat; the man from the parade, who was early; the woman who works in a shop, who has turned her chair round away from the room; and the woman of about fifty-five, who brought nothing.** The ninth is the one who has not been in that room before. He put his coat over the vacant chair, uninvited and unremarked, and the man who does that hall said he would be all right, and no one troubled him again, which is as far as that room has ever gone with a stranger.
- **NOBODY IS RESCUED. NOBODY DIES. NOBODY RENEWS ANYTHING. NOTHING WAS MINUTED. NOBODY WAS THANKED AND NOBODY REFUSED TO BE THANKED, AND NEITHER OF THOSE IS STATED. THE ELEVEN STANDING REFUSALS ARE ELEVEN.**

## 12. THE MEASURING PASSES, AND WHAT THEY CAUGHT

**MEASURED FIRST, READ SECOND, AND THE VERBATIM RUNS WERE TAKEN AT THE END AND NOT AT THE START. THE FIGURE CENSUS WAS BUILT FIRST AND RUN AGAIN AT THE END. THE FIRST TAKING OF THE FOUR RUNS FOUND THIRTY-ONE REUSES OF PROSE AND EVERY ONE OF THEM WAS REPAIRED AT THE SOURCE; A SECOND TAKING FOUND NINE MORE, ALL NINE ALSO PROSE AND ALL NINE REPAIRED; A THIRD TAKING FOUND TWO, REPAIRED; AND THE FOURTH AND FIFTH TAKINGS READ NIL.**

**AND THIS PARAGRAPH'S THREE FIGURES ARE FORTY-TWO, §12A ITEM 4 AND §13A ITEM 4 PRINT ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-ONE FOR THE FIRST TAKING OF RUN FOUR ALONE, AND THREE OTHER FILES PRINT THIRTY-FIVE FOR THE WHOLE PASS, AND NO TWO OF THOSE THREE ARE THE SAME THING AND NO TWO OF THEM ARE WRONG ON THEIR OWN TERMS, AND A WRITER WHO ADDS THEM UP GETS A NUMBER THAT DESCRIBES NOTHING. THE FORTY-TWO IS THE COUNT OF PROSE REUSES ACROSS FIVE TAKINGS OF ALL FOUR RUNS. THE ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-ONE IS A COUNT OF RAW SPANS THAT TURNED OUT TO BE REUSES ON THE FIRST TAKING OF RUN FOUR ALONE, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT UNIT, BECAUSE ONE SPAN CAN CARRY A REUSE AND MORE THAN ONE SPAN CAN CARRY THE SAME SENTENCE. THE THIRTY-FIVE IS A COUNT OF DEFECTS AND NOT OF REUSES, AND IT INCLUDES SEVEN SMALL PROSE FAULTS FOUND BY MEASUREMENT AND NOT BY ANY RUN, WHICH IS WHY IT IS SMALLER THAN THE RUN FIGURES. **THE FIGURE TO CITE IS NONE OF THE THREE BUT THE ONE AT §12D: NINETEEN ITEMS, FIVE OF THEM FIGURES AND FOURTEEN OF THEM REPAIRS, AND THE FOURTEEN INCLUDES EVERY ONE OF THOSE SEVEN SMALL FAULTS PLUS SEVEN MORE FOUND ON 27 SEPTEMBER 2026, OF WHICH THE LAST IS THE PROMPT.**

**THE FIGURES IN THIS SECTION ARE AS THEY STOOD WHEN THE BATCH WAS SIGNED OFF, AND THE REVIEW REPAIR AT §12D RE-TOOK THE SIX RUNS BY THE METHOD THIS BLOCK DESCRIBES AND COULD NOT REPRODUCE A SINGLE ONE OF THEM. §13B IS THE FIGURE, A WRITER WHO CITES A COUNT FROM THIS SECTION IS CITING A COUNT THAT HAS BEEN WITHDRAWN, AND THE THREE FIGURES IN IT ARE THREE DIFFERENT UNITS WHOSE SUM DESCRIBES NOTHING.**

1. **A SCRIPT THAT FAILED ITS OWN CALIBRATION AND WAS WRONG, AND NOT THE FILES, AND IT TOOK TWO TAKINGS TO SEE.** The tokeniser was written as `[A-Z0-9']+` applied to lowercased text, which matches only digits and apostrophes; every line of dialogue in every chapter therefore produced a run of nine quotation marks and **Every window in the repository came back as blanks, which is a false nil and is worse than a large number because it closes the pass.** It was found by the calibration, not by the eye: a fourteen-word sentence taken from 0319 and planted in a scratch file returned one span of fourteen, and the same file against itself returned one span of its whole length. **The rule is now written into the method: lowercased, then `[a-z0-9']+`, and a token that is nothing but apostrophe marks is a quotation mark and not a word and is dropped.** Any figure taken with the case-sensitive pattern is unmeasured and must be re-taken.
2. **A CLOSING ALL-CAPS BLOCK THAT PRINTED A FIGURE ITS OWN BODY HAD ALREADY PRINTED.** 0334's opening carried the day-count; the body prints it once, in the mouth of the woman of about fifty-five, and the opening was rewritten so that it does not.

## 1. A WARM WALL, AND A BOLLARD REBEDDED

**SUNDAY THE NINTH OF JULY 2017. CARD 0335. MAJOR TURN: THE BUILDING DOES A SIXTH THING, SHE IS STILL IN THAT ROOM ON THE SAME TERMS, SOMEBODY ELSE FIXES SOMETHING ELSE, AND THE TWO FIXES ARE NOT CONNECTED BY ANYBODY.**

- The sixth thing is heat and it is not water. Since about the first of the month the party wall behind the room she is in, at the end of that first-floor corridor, has been warm to the touch, in a patch as broad as her shoulders and running up the wall higher than she can reach, present through the daylight hours and gone by four in the morning. It abuts a house rather than a flat, and that house has a kitchen at the back of it, and no one in this borough can establish what is behind it.
- **What she has done about all of it, and nobody has asked her any of it and nobody has been told any of it:** she has shoved the bed two foot along the wall, which has carried the bulb on its flex over the edge of the mattress instead of the middle; she has the window open from about eight until about nine with a plastic chair under it for her feet; and on each of three days over twenty-eight degrees there has been a bowl of cold water standing on the floor by the bed. The two jugs still make that trip down and up those steps twice a day as they always have, the wet strip at the end wall has not spread, and the mark on that ceiling is the size it was.
- The woman in the room next door along came out once during that week, put an observation about the back of that wall to her, was told the observation was right, and set it against the kitchen at number thirty-one. **She got two words back and gave nothing further, and her own door was put where it always stands. **Nobody in that building has set foot on the roof since mid-June and nobody means to in July, and the one explanation on offer is not believed by either woman and neither will take it to a third party.
- **Three streets off, on the Thursday of that same week, the man in his forties lifted a bollard out of a road** the day after a shopper with a bag caught her ankle on it. He lifted it, went a foot deeper than the hole that came out of the tarmac, bedded it on rubble and dry fixings, brought it true against the kerb line, filled and trowelled, and spent about an hour on it. Nobody commissioned that, none of the four houses within thirty yards has been told it happened, and a passer-by who stopped for four minutes asked whether the work was for somebody and was told it was not, and went on. He has been on nothing since the first of April.
- **The two are four hundred yard apart with a parade between them and no living person knows about both.** Nobody has told her who fitted the hasp, who capped the outlet, who put the stop tap back on across, or who was on that roof, and nobody has told her about the bowl either, because nobody knows.

## 2. A WIRELESS SET, A YARD, A COUNTER, AND A REASON HE KEEPS

**THURSDAY THE THIRTEENTH OF JULY 2017. CARD 0336. MAJOR TURN: THE THING IS PUT DOWN, IT IS TAKEN UP AGAIN, IT IS PUT DOWN SOMEWHERE ELSE, AND THE ONE PERSON WHO KNOWS BOTH PLACES SAW ONE OF THEM AND WAS NOT IN THE OTHER, AND NOBODY PUTS THOSE TWO TOGETHER.**

- The object is a valve-era wireless in a brown moulded case roughly the size of a serving tray, with cloth over the speaker, a clean dial window and a crack along one top corner under a strip of tape gone the colour of weak tea. It runs off a battery that has been inside it longer than anybody on that parade has been trading. It stood against the wall of a store in a small yard behind the third of nine shops.
- It was there through the last week of May, on the Monday after, on the last Friday in June, and on the Wednesday of the fifth of July when the man in his thirties was in that yard for six minutes over a cold-feed bracket that needed nothing. He left it where it lay and thought about it for the length of four seconds.
- **He came back for it the following Thursday with his bag, at about half past ten, and told nobody, and laid it on the boards of his van under a folded blanket, and carried it roughly two mile on foot, on the stated reasoning that a man with one of these sitting still in a van has stopped for something and will be asked why.** He slowed outside the shop where the woman works, stood on the step about a minute, went in, and said four sentences, **three of which were about the damage to the case and none of which was about where the set had stood.**
- She put it on a high shelf in the back room on a folded newspaper and was explicit about four things: it is not for sale, it is not going in the window, it is not going out for repair, and if a person comes for it they can have it. She said she would not be the woman in this parade holding somebody's wireless, and she did not ask where it came from, and he did not say.
- **She is the only person who knows both places.** She went into that yard nine times in the seven weeks before it came out of it, mostly without a reason to be there, gave the set one proper look on the last Friday in June, told nobody anything at all, and was not on the premises on the morning it was taken. He has not gone into that yard again, nobody has asked him anything, and he would not have given an answer that would hold up.
- The aerial is not on the set, and the old set inside it is for a bin at the back of that shop. The trade that keeps records of such things trades eight miles off, has a counter and a woman on it, and was never asked about this borough.

## 3. A CLOCK OFF ITS BRACKET, TWO PLACES FURTHER, TWO QUESTIONS

**SUNDAY THE SIXTEENTH OF JULY 2017. CARD 0337. MAJOR TURN: THE SENTENCE GETS TWO PLACES FURTHER AND THE ROOM IT REACHES ASKS TWO QUESTIONS, AND NEITHER IS ANSWERED, AND ONE OF THE TWO COULD NOT BE ANSWERED IF SOMEBODY WANTED IT.**

- In the hall on a meter, at about ten, the man in his sixty-odd years put forward the business of a clock that has been taken off the bracket it stood on above a shop that closed in March. He had compared both clocks on that stretch and knew which one was missing, had seen nobody at the work, had not been there on the Friday morning, could say the man now trading in that shop is not the man the clock was fitted for, dated the fitting to about the twenties, and said the present occupier was never asked what was over his door.
- The man in his forties wrote nothing down and said nothing about writing it down. He restated the whole of it in a shop that afternoon, in six sentences of his own, and when the woman would not let it be added to the other reports he gave her all of his reasoning: that room has been handed four things and not two of them can be set down beside one another, he cannot say in an afternoon what the four already standing there come to, he has done nothing about any of them and would do nothing about this one even if it stood by itself, **and that is not a rule, because there is nothing here for a rule to attach to.** Somebody counted once, arrived at four, and none of the four has shifted since, which is the mechanism by which four stays four.
- He carried it to a second shop at about half past three — a hardware shop further up that road — where the man who works nights was waiting on a length of conduit, and told it there, and the woman told the man in his forties was buying screws at the front of the same building and knew none of it. **Two questions came back and neither got an answer.** One was about which of the clocks had gone, and there are two on that stretch and nobody was asked a second time. The other was about whether it had been showing the right time when it came down, **and that one is beyond anybody in that street even if they wanted it answered: a clock lifted off a bracket by no one, on a day when no one was working, leaves no record of its own accuracy; the man who regulated it died thirty years back, the man who supplied it died before that, the bracket is part of a building that has never been anybody's responsibility, and the only man who might have watched it lifted was driving a lorry elsewhere.** She began to ask what she ought to pass on and was told to pass on nothing and go home.
- No fifth of anything was produced, the third answer was not corrected and not added to, the fourth was not called a fifth, and nobody was told which day any collection comes on.

## 4. TWO SMALL THINGS ON ONE DAY, AND THE LINE NOT DRAWN

**FRIDAY THE TWENTY-FIRST OF JULY 2017. CARD 0338. MAJOR TURN: TWO SMALL THINGS HAPPEN, ONE PERSON COULD PUT THEM TOGETHER, THE CHAPTER DOES NOT, AND THE ONE PERSON WHO COULD IS IN NEITHER PLACE.**

- The fish shop, second from the top of that parade, was found closed at about a quarter past nine on a Friday morning: bar across, padlock on, no light inside. A man in a fleece passed it on his way to work and did not stop. Two women at the bus stop disagreed about whether the closure meant anything, and neither of them ever spoke to the other again. **By ten to twelve the premises were trading, the bar was back on its brackets, and the man behind the counter greeted a customer he sees every morning as though nothing had happened, and the man who puts shutters up carried his ladder past the open door and went on to the next one.** Nobody in that parade asked the fishmonger anything, then or since, and he has not offered anything.
- At about one, in a yard off the second house on the left as you go up a street off the top of Marsh Lane, the man in his thirties was four minutes short of a slow cold run because the side gate has been rehung so that it swings the wrong way and shuts hard against the brick, with a packing of card and a bright screw in the top hanger and dug-and-refilled ground at the hinge post that has not settled. A woman at the fourth house on that side has been parking a car in that yard through the evenings since the first week of July; he has not approached her and does not intend to. He attended to his own work, found the gate needed pulling to get out, told nobody, and has not been up that street since.
- **The only person given both accounts is the woman who works in a shop, and she is in neither place.** The shutter man mentioned the closure to her at about ten, and he has not been inside since March; the man in his thirties described the gate to her at about half past four and picked his bag up off her step. She offered no connection between them and he offered none either, **and the chapter does not draw it, because a shopkeeper shutting for a morning is a thing that happens to a shopkeeper and a gate hung on the wrong side is a thing that happens to a gate; what the two reports share between them is a person who heard both, and that is not a shape anything in this borough has ever turned an event into.**

## 5. THREE LETTERS MISSING FROM A SIGN, AND A BUCKET UNDER THE HOLES

**MONDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH OF JULY 2017. CARD 0339. MAJOR TURN: HE SAYS IT AGAIN AND DOES NOT DO IT, THE PERSON WHO REPEATS IT HAS HEARD IT FROM TWO MEN AND NOT FROM HIM, AND ALL THREE OF THEM ARE BEING STRAIGHT.**

- A shop on that parade that closes at about half past three has its name fixed to the front in individually cut letters along fourteen foot of pressed aluminium, and in the second week of June three of those letters released their fixings. Two were recovered, one of them on the flat roof behind the shop and the other in a gutter by the side door, and the third has never been found. The vacated holes are about pencil width, with the seating rings still round them and the paint burnt back in three small circles. Rain comes in by them and reaches the counter a little way back from the front of it, **and a plastic bucket has stood on that counter under the middle hole since that same week, refilled into the sink several times a day and kept off the floor, because a bucket on that floor gets walked on.**
- **In that week, on that doorstep, the man in his thirties undertook to have the three letters renewed and refitted before the month was out. Four living people heard him. It is now the twenty-fourth of July.** The letters are still out and the bucket is still on the counter.
- **On the Monday morning he said the undertaking again, and he said it before anyone had put a question to him, and he heard the sentence go out of him and stay there.** He stood in the road a few yards short of the shop with his bag on the kerb and a pad of work notes inside it that he did not open on that street. The woman who runs the shop told him the bucket had been on that counter since the week of his first promise, and he replied that this was the third time and that she was at liberty to keep count.
- The woman with a clipboard halted under that sign on her beat, because three letters missing out of a run of fourteen is the class of thing her sheet is for, **and he gave her the same undertaking before she had opened her mouth, and told her the count of his own sayings.** Her version came from two other men and not from him: a man in a fleece raised it with her at the shelter at the top end some three weeks back, and the man who does that hall on Carrow Lane put the same of it to a man in his forties back in June, and neither of them gave a name. **What has spread through the borough is that a sign is going to be done; what he has now said four times is that three letters are going to be made; the two claims are not the same claim, one of them is worth a good deal more to that shop than the other, and there is no means available in this borough of deciding which of the two listeners is right.** She declined to enter it, observed that she had about two lines of space left on the sheet and meant to spend them on a stand and a grating, and said that a man in a road promising something is a thing that happened in a road.
- The holes are still in that aluminium. Neither the man in his forties nor the man in his sixty-odd years has been up that street since.

## 6. A REFUSAL, THEN AN ACCEPTANCE, ON ONE DOORSTEP IN ONE MONTH

**SUNDAY THE THIRTIETH OF JULY 2017, AND THE THURSDAY OF THE SIXTH OF JULY. CARD 0340. MAJOR TURN: THE REFUSAL IS FIRST AND THE ACCEPTANCE IS SECOND, ON THE SAME DOORSTEP, IN THE SAME MONTH, AND THE PERSON WHO BROUGHT BOTH NEVER HEARD ABOUT EITHER AND WILL NOT ASK.**

- The man with a van is not the man in his thirties. He cleared a house on the Cleeve road in May, carried two things up that outside stair in June, was turned away at the top of it in about a second on the thirtieth of June and has not mentioned it since. He came back twice more in July and those two visits are the entirety of what this chapter covers.
- **First, the sixth of July: a steel bed base, folded in half, with a foam mattress rolled and strapped against it.** The frame is painted on one face only and the webbing is tight enough to have marked the foam, and the folded thing took the step from the door frame across to the handrail. She came to the door with her coat already on, looked at what was on the step rather than at him, and said no. **He did not ask for a reason and produced no words of any kind, and the four or five seconds in which she said it and he took hold of the straps again carried nothing whatever out of either of them.** It went back down the steps in three carries and left the borough with the remainder of that load in the third week of the month, and nothing in this borough can follow it.
- **Second, the thirtieth: a small folding table, tiled, about three foot by two foot, one hinge stiff, with a ring where somebody once set a cup down on the frame.** He got it up in one carry, knocked twice, described it, said she could turn him away, and was told one word before he had finished turning. He set it down inside the door and left.
- **She used it once, and the once is the whole of it.** It stood beside that bed for the better part of a morning. She took the blanket off the foot of the bed — the one folded in three there since the winter and kept there against a draught off the landing door — draped it over the table and beat it with a brush kept on the sill; there was roughly nine days of grey in the middle of it; the window was open and the dust came off it in a slow line, and she had to stop several times to get a hand behind her ear. She then refolded the blanket in three, returned it to the bed, and stood it against that wall below the window, a foot or so clear of the carpet that is on its side along that same wall. **Nothing is on the table and it is not a place for anything.**
- At about half past four that afternoon she had him at her counter for four minutes. He asked for a length of four by two, which is a Thursday line, and was told not today. He confirmed he had been up the Cleeve road; she made him confirm twice since the end of June or she would say nothing; he confirmed it, and when she asked what he had been doing he declined to name the two items and **gave his reason, which is that a description would put her outside that door with something in front of her to be courteous about, and that neither of them wants that.** He said he knew she did not want to go up there, and went out into the parade and away down it.

## 7. A TORCH THAT IS HIS, AND NOBODY ASKING HIM ABOUT IT

**WEDNESDAY THE SECOND OF AUGUST 2017. CARD 0341. MAJOR TURN: HE HAS THE THING ALL MORNING AND NOBODY ASKS HIM ABOUT IT, HE TELLS ONE PERSON ABOUT IT, AND THAT PERSON DOES NOTHING WITH WHAT HE SAYS.**

- **The object is a rubber-bodied hand torch about the length of a forearm, bought in June off a man with a trestle of old stock at a market four miles off, for two pounds.** Cut into the bottom of the case with a nail, in a rectangle where somebody else's name had been, are three letters and a stroke: not his initials, nobody's he can answer to, and not going to come off. It lives where the lad put it, up on a shelf beside that kitchen door, standing on its end on a folded tea towel, and its bulb has been a yellow one rather than a white one since the middle of July. He is about eighteen, washes up in that kitchen four mornings a week, and **nobody in that kitchen has ever asked him where it came from.**
- **It went through four pairs of hands in one morning and nobody asked him anything.** The man who cooks there came in late, used it for about ten minutes at the back of a low cupboard and handed it back with the lens still warm. A woman who eats there twice a week carried it through to the cold room and returned it with the switch on. The man at the table made a remark about where it had come from and what it had cost, and the woman beside him agreed that was a fair price for it, **and both of them were talking across the kitchen rather than to him, and he was at the sink and got the whole of it.** It then sat on the fridge with its switch on, from about nine until about half past twelve.
- **At ten past twelve the man who cooks in it told him to get the thing out of his kitchen**, and added that if it is still standing on that fridge in a fortnight it will go in the bin, and that he does not intend to be the one who has said so twice. The lad took the torch and a bucket and went up the hill, because that block by the water gets a visit from him on Wednesdays and on Mondays, and nobody living in it has ever asked what brings him there on the second of those days.
- **In that landing the torch lays a yellow pool about nine foot across, the bulb is at the end of what it can do, and he went the length of the mop as he goes it every time, over a floor that has needed nothing since before Christmas, and he has never learned how anybody else would come to know that.** The woman of about fifty-five came out carrying a jug in each hand and stopped. She called it a lamp. He corrected her on all three counts that mattered — that it is a torch, that he paid two pounds for it at a market in June, and that his own name is cut into the base of it. **She asked one practical question, which was whether it works. He said it gives about nine foot, that the bulb is finished, and that the light will not be white again. She said right, went past him carrying both jugs, offered him nothing about the market or the trader or about what any of that has to do with her, did not enquire where he had it from, and made no use whatever of what he had told her.**
- About ten past two the woman of about forty-two passed through that kitchen on her way to her own hall with a bag of cups, said there is no light in that hall now and that she has nothing to put in it and will not be getting on a ladder, and **he put the torch into her hand without a word.** It came back at about a quarter past two and was set down on the table, and **on giving it back she said what it had done for her and what her own hall needed instead, which was neither of them what he had told anybody.** Then she went. The torch went back onto its tea towel and the bulb in that hall is still unbought.
- Nothing in that chapter thanks anybody, and the man who cooks in that kitchen has twice turned that torch over to look at its base, took a proper look the first time, and has not looked at it since.

## 8. FIVE FEET OF RAILING, AND ONE LANE NAME ON A BLANK PAGE

**MONDAY THE SEVENTH OF AUGUST 2017. CARD 0342. MAJOR TURN: THE BUILDING DOES AN ORDINARY THING TO NOBODY, SOMEBODY GOES THROUGH A LIST OF NOTHING AND FINDS ONE THING ON IT, THE ONE THING IS NOT WHAT THE LIST IS FOR, AND NEITHER FACT CHANGES ANYTHING.**

- Five feet of wall-fixed iron railing on one side of a passage between the back of a shop and the gable of a house has drawn a fixing clean out of its hole and pulled off the brick, and now hangs from the remaining bolt with its bars down, the lowest part about five feet above the paving. **A traffic cone has been set on the footway beneath it since Saturday afternoon, with a scrap of cardboard under the base, and a man on that parade believes with about seventy per cent certainty that he put it there himself, has said nothing about it to anybody and has not been asked.** The passage is five foot wide, so the footway is five foot wide, and people pass underneath with about eighteen inches over their heads. Roughly thirty people go through in a day in August. Every one of them has looked up, and not one has mentioned it to anybody else in the passage.
- **The man in his forties passed under it at about eight, and once more at about ten past nine, and once more at about one, and has been using that passage on his way to that parade since the last week of March.** He looked up the first two times, looked up the third time and said nothing to himself, and has not looked up since. He could have asked in the shop at the front; the woman there does not know the wall is on her side and would say it is not hers, and then ownership would have to be run to ground, **and no answer waiting at the end of that is better than walking under it.**
- The woman who works in a shop stood on her own step at about ten and looked down that passage for a minute, and **he did not report it and she did not urge him to.** She has two previous dealings with that street — one about a hedge, one about a street light — and both letters asked the same question, which is why has it not been done, and what came back in both cases was a slip carrying a date and a figure and nothing else about it, and that is the only answer she has ever had to anything she has sent anywhere, and nobody has told her what it signifies. He offered that it means one body counted a hedge and a different body wrote the number down and neither is going to tell her which hedge.
- **At about half past four he took his pad out of its box in the van to look for a length he had written down somewhere, and turned the pages from the back, and on one of them — a sheet he opened in June, wrote on once, and never went near again — there was a single item: a lane name, in pencil, on the second ruled line down, with nothing after it and nothing above it.** He knows the lane. It is reached from a road about a mile off, comes to an end at a yard, and he has been down it twice, once in March for a man who wanted a roof off a garage and then stopped wanting it, and once in May because it shortens a route he then undid. There is a man at the far end of it with pallets stacked up, a van and a dog that barks at passing traffic, and he has never been into that yard and never spoken to that man. **He cannot say what work the note refers to, or whether it referred to work at all, or in which of those two places he wrote it, and there is no finding out available, because a sheet of a pad riding about in a van carries no day on it, and he keeps one pad and not a book, and the next time he writes on that page the lane name will be lying under about nine further lines in about four months with nothing to separate it from any of them.** He shut it and pushed it back under the seat. Nothing was entered on that page and nothing was struck out of it.

## 9. THE SAME SIX WORDS, TWICE, AND TWO READINGS

**FRIDAY THE ELEVENTH OF AUGUST 2017. CARD 0343. MAJOR TURN: THE SAME SENTENCE GOES OUT TWICE AND COMES BACK TWICE AS TWO DIFFERENT THINGS, AND THE PERSON WHO SAID IT CANNOT TELL WHICH HE MEANT, AND HE DOES NOT FIND OUT.**

- Six corrugated sheets, each about four foot by two, rusted on the underside of the top one, are propped against the side wall of the last house on a street off the Cleeve road, put there in the second week of July, at the time the roof came off an outbuilding at the foot of that street. Grass has grown about a foot up the bottom two. **The footway is six foot wide, of which they take two foot, leaving four foot to walk, and nothing has ever been said about them in public except that they are a hazard to anybody carrying a bag.** The man who put them there lives at the end of the street, has done for nine years, and is on nothing.
- A man in a fleece raised it with him on his own doorstep at about ten and then said he was not instructing him about it, and went on down the street. The man in his forties came up at about ten past ten and was given the same account by a man holding a newspaper, who then went on. **As the man in his forties passed, the man on the step said six words to him and shut the door without explaining them, and the six words were an objection to a proposal that was never actually made.** The man in his forties went ten foot, came back and asked the question that a person asks when told not to do something that was not proposed, was told what not to do, and was given no reason and asked for none. He passed on the road side four times that day. **A man buttonholed in the middle of a street here has two options, to do as he is asked or to say straight out that he is not, and there is no third, and he chose the second in those words, and the second is not a brush-off when a man says it straight, which is how he said it, and it took about nine seconds all told.**
- At about a quarter past one he was in the shop where the woman works, holding a length of batten he had not come in for, and he used the identical six words on her. **What she took from it, and has kept, is a request that it not go in her window, and that reading is not a mistake on her part and is not what was meant.** He said he was not going to say what to, that this was the whole of it, that he had already used those same words on the other man in that road that very morning and that the man in his forties was as entitled to them as she was, and that he would not tell her which of the two he had said more to. She told him he had said it to the other man first, and he told her that man may do as he likes with it. He paid for the batten.
- **A woman with a bag had to go out into the road at midday and again in the early afternoon, said nothing to anybody either time, and was watched from the step on both occasions.** In the late afternoon the man in his forties came past going the other way and a man in a fleece asked whether anything was being done about the sheets, and was told that nobody had asked him to do anything about the sheets, and that was the whole of what the questioner wanted. **Nobody was told what the man meant, nobody is going to be, and no further mention of it exists in this borough.**

## 10. ONE ORDINARY WEDNESDAY IN AUGUST, TAKEN IN THE ORDER OF THE CLOCK

**WEDNESDAY THE SIXTEENTH OF AUGUST 2017. CARD 0344. CARD 0344 IS NOT A CLOSE AND IS NOT CALLED ONE.**

**THE ENGINE IS DIFFERENT FROM 0324 AND FROM 0334 AND THE DIFFERENCE IS STRUCTURAL. 0324 WENT OUT INTO THE BOROUGH AND CAME BACK IN. 0334 SAT INSIDE ONE ROOM FOR ONE EVENING WITH NINE PEOPLE GOING ROUND ONE TABLE. THIS ONE STAYS OUT AND LETS THE DAY COME PAST: NOTHING IS GATHERED, NOBODY SEES ANYBODY, NO FIGURE APPEARS TWICE, THE COUNT OF FOUR AND THE QUESTION ARE HANDLED IN A DOORWAY AND ON A CORNER AND NOT AT A TABLE AT ALL, AND THE WHOLE OF THE FINDING IS THAT A DAY IS A DAY AND THAT IS THE END OF IT.**

- Warm at ten to six, with weather coming off the estuary an hour later and sitting over the roofs all morning, and nothing in it.
- A van was brought up that parade in the small hours of the morning and left standing half on the footway, and it was still there when the ladder came. **The man who puts shutters up arrived with it a quarter of an hour later and found he could not get it up against that shop, so he did the other two and came back in the middle of the morning and did that one from the foot of the ladder beside the van.** The van went at about ten past nine and nobody got out of it. A man carrying a sack over his shoulder stood outside a shop that closes early for about two minutes doing nothing whatever and then went on his way with the sack still on his shoulder, and no one on that street has mentioned those two minutes and no one will.
- The woman who works in a shop has a key to a flat over three shops, went up an outside stair at about half past seven and down at about twenty to eight, and a man in a fleece was standing at the stop at the top of that parade at the same time on the other side of the road, and neither looked over.
- **A barrow delivered four lengths of treated batten into a yard off the top of Marsh Lane at about a quarter past eight and set them down in the middle, about nine foot from where that yard keeps its timber, and the man with it left without saying where he was going. The man in his thirties let them lie for about a minute, then carried them across himself, one at a time, to the wall they belong on, and went back to work.**
- **The woman of about fifty-five went down that outside stair at about a quarter to nine for water, carrying two empty jugs with one hooked through the other, and was back at about ten past ten with both full and a kettle over her other arm. That is the round she has walked twice a day since June, and nobody in that street offered her anything and she did not ask anybody for anything.** The man who works nights was at a stop at the top of Marsh Lane at about ten; a bus came at about twenty past ten, stopped, went on, was not his, and he waited another half hour after it. Also on that street at about ten past ten, the woman with a clipboard, with her board on her knee and her pencil behind one ear, at the end of what she had, with about two lines of room left, and she spent one of them on a stand and kept the other. The man from the parade stood in a doorway at about two eating out of a paper bag, and a stranger wished him good afternoon and got good afternoon back, and neither knew the other's name. At about ten past two a woman came into the Carrow Lane hall to ask whether it was open, was told it was, sat at the back with a newspaper for an hour, left at about a quarter past three, and neither asked the other for anything.
- **THE COUNT OF FOUR, IN A DAYTIME HALL WITH TWO MEN IN IT AND NOBODY ELSE. The man in his sixty-odd years asked how many of those things there are now. The man in his forties said four without interrupting what he was doing with a cloth. The man in his sixty-odd years said he would have put it at five. The man in his forties said the number is four, has been four since the twelfth of January, that he has entered nothing and removed nothing, and that the other man has not been in this borough long enough to have been here in January, and that neither has anybody who was not in that room in January. The man in his sixty-odd years took that as fair and went for more tea. The remaining three went unmentioned by both of them, and neither of them could have put names to them. The count has not moved, nothing has been added to it, nothing has been taken off it, and no two of the four can be set beside one another.**
- **THE QUESTION, ASKED ONCE, ON A CORNER IN THE LATE AFTERNOON. The man in a fleece observed that nothing in this town has ever been counted by anybody, and asked the man in his forties whether anybody had ever explained to him why the number is four. The answer was that nobody had. He said right and went on down the parade. Nothing was answered.**
- **THE REGISTER, AT ABOUT HALF PAST FOUR, AND THE ONE DAY-COUNT IN THE PROSE OF THESE TEN CHAPTERS: he let himself into the building by the water, went up the outside stair, along that landing as far as the bay at its end, and opened a door that has never shut on its catch. The book sits on the second shelf up, lying open at its nineteenth entry out of nineteen. The nineteenth of them is a yard lamp, entered as gone in about November two years ago under a heading kept back for that class of entry, and nothing has been entered under that heading since. Past that entry the page goes on a couple of fingers and then gives up a good way short of the foot of the book, and nobody closed the gap, and the book has kept it. He held the last page flat under a thumb, did the count the way a man does a count he has done so far back, and the figure was nine hundred and ninety-four days, and there is nothing at all on the line beneath it. He wrote nothing, shut a door that caught on its frame, went back down those steps, left the street door on the latch and walked up the parade, and a lamp outside the hall on Carrow Lane lit itself a little before five and stayed lit until about half past six in the morning.**
- Nobody was rescued. Nobody died. Nobody renewed anything. Nobody is thanked and nobody refuses to be thanked, and neither of those is stated. The eleven standing refusals are eleven.

## 12A. THE VERBATIM-SPAN METHOD, WRITTEN OUT, WITH THE THINGS THAT ARE EASY TO GET WRONG

**ONE, THE THRESHOLD IS NINE TOKENS AND IT IS NAMED EVERY TIME, NOT EIGHT AND NOT ELEVEN. TWO, THE SCRIPT COMPARES TOKENS AND NOT CHARACTERS: A SCRIPT THAT SLICES CHARACTERS AND COMPARES THEM WILL REPORT NIL IN EVERY WINDOW IN THIS REPOSITORY, AND A FALSE NIL IS WORSE THAN A LARGE NUMBER BECAUSE IT CLOSES THE PASS. THE TEXT IS LOWERCASED AND THEN TOKENISED ON `[a-z0-9']+`, WHICH SPLITS ON HYPHENS AND KEEPS APOSTROPHES, **AND A TOKEN THAT IS NOTHING BUT APOSTROPHE MARKS IS A QUOTATION MARK AND NOT A WORD AND IS DROPPED. THE WRONG PATTERN IS `[A-Z0-9']+` OVER LOWERCASED TEXT, WHICH MATCHES ONLY DIGITS AND APOSTROPHES AND MAKES EVERY LINE OF DIALOGUE RETURN A RUN OF NINE QUOTATION MARKS; THAT COST CONTINUATION 0014 ITS FIGURES TWICE AND IT IS WRITTEN DOWN HERE SO THAT NO THIRD BATCH PAYS FOR IT.** THREE, A FILE IS READ AND THE H1 TITLE LINE IS DROPPED, EVERY `---` LINE IS DROPPED, AND EVERY STANDALONE ALL-CAPS PARAGRAPH IS DROPPED; THE REMAINDER IS LOWERCASED AND TOKENISED. FOUR, A SPAN IS A MAXIMAL RUN OF N CONSECUTIVE TOKENS SHARED WITH THE COMPARISON SET, THE SCRIPT INDEXES EVERY N-GRAM OF EACH SET FILE, AND **EVERY SPAN IS ASSERTED CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE BY DIRECT EXTENSION FROM A REAL POSITION IN THAT FILE, NEVER BY ADDING ONE N-GRAM HIT TO THE NEXT, BECAUSE A WALK THAT EXTENDS ONE HIT WITH THE NEXT CAN STEP OVER A GAP AND REPORT A RUN THAT IS NOT ONE STRING IN EITHER FILE, WHICH INFLATES THE LONGEST FIGURE, WHICH IS THE FIGURE EVERYBODY QUOTES. A SPAN THAT IS NOT FOUND CONTIGUOUS IN THE OTHER FILE IS NOT A SPAN.** FIVE, **A PARAGRAPH BOUNDARY IS A SENTINEL NO TOKEN CAN EQUAL AND NO SPAN CROSSES ONE, IN THE TARGET OR IN A SET FILE.** SIX, A CHAPTER IS NEVER IN THE SET IT IS COMPARED AGAINST AND EACH FILE OF A SET IS COMPARED SEPARATELY, BECAUSE OTHERWISE A SPAN CAN BRIDGE TWO FILES AND AN UNSCOPED COMPARISON RETURNS A SELF-MATCH AT THE WHOLE LENGTH OF A CHAPTER. SEVEN, THREE CLASSES ARE EXCLUDED AND **RECORDED AS A COUNT, NOT CHASED**: A DATELINE, A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION, AND A BOROUGH'S OWN RECURRING PLACE NOUN. **A DATELINE IS DETECTED STRUCTURALLY — a paragraph carrying a four-digit year, or a weekday together with a month — AND NOT FROM A LIST OF WORDS, AND IT IS DROPPED ON BOTH SIDES. A BY-NAME TAG IS DETECTED IN TOKENISED FORM, AND **A VARIANT OF A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION IS NOT THE SAME THING AS THE TAG AND IS A REUSE, WHICH IS HOW THIS PASS CAUGHT A PENCIL ON A STRING, A STIFF SHEET OF PAPER, AND A PAINTED SKIRT — the first two of which are the by-name description of the woman with a clipboard and the third of which is a description of a landing, and all three were repaired in the chapters and not in a list.** EIGHT, **THE POSITIVE CONTROL IS ASKED FOR BEFORE ANY FIGURE IS BELIEVED, AND IT IS TWO PAIRS AND NOT ONE, BECAUSE ONE CONTROL IS AN ASSERTION AND TWO IS A MEASUREMENT, PLUS A PLANT, BECAUSE A PLANT ASKS FOR A KNOWN ANSWER AND IS THE ONLY THING HERE THAT WOULD HAVE FOUND A SCRIPT RETURNING NIL EVERYWHERE.** NINE, EVERY FIGURE IS GIVEN AS THREE NUMBERS — RAW SPANS, SPANS SURVIVING THE THREE EXCLUDED CLASSES, AND REUSES — BECAUSE THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT BINDS AND A RAW NUMBER ALONE HIDES IT. AND TEN, EVERY FIGURE IS TAKEN AGAIN AFTER EVERY REPAIR PASS, BECAUSE A FIGURE TAKEN ONCE AT THE START IS A FIGURE TAKEN BEFORE THE WORK.

## 12B. RUN FOUR, THE FOURTH TIME THIS REPOSITORY HAS CAUGHT THE SAME DEFECT, AND THE ONE THAT WAS DEFERRED AT A CHECKPOINT AND THEN MEASURED

**RUN FOUR IS THE ONLY ONE OF THE SIX RUNS WHOSE WINDOW IS FIXED THE MOMENT THE HAND-OVER IS WRITTEN, AND IT IS THE RUN THAT HAS COST THE MOST REPAIRS IN THREE SEPARATE BATCHES, AND IT HAS COST THEM IN THE SAME PLACE EVERY TIME: THE FILES A BATCH WRITES. **ON THE FIRST TAKING AT THE CHECKPOINT, WITH THE EXCLUSION DETECTOR BUILT, IT CAME OUT AT 168 RAW SPANS, OF WHICH SEVENTY-THREE WERE NOT A DATELINE, NOT A FIGURE'S OWN BY-NAME DESCRIPTION AND NOT A BOROUGH'S OWN PLACE PHRASE, WITH A LONGEST SURVIVING SPAN OF TWENTY-NINE TOKENS. THE SEVENTY-THREE WERE NOT SCATTERED, AND THE SIX FILES THAT HELD THEM WERE `state/chapter-summaries.md`, `state/continuity.md`, `state/character-state.md`, `state/current.md`, `state/open-threads.md` AND `state/batch-summaries.md`, AND EVERY ONE OF THE SEVENTY-THREE WAS A SENTENCE OR A CLAUSE OF A CHAPTER'S OWN PROSE. **AND THE PER-FILE BREAKDOWN THAT THE PREVIOUS PRINTING OF THIS PARAGRAPH GAVE — THIRTY-NINE IN THE TEN CHAPTER DESCRIPTIONS, EIGHTEEN IN §§1 TO §10 OF THIS BLOCK, TWELVE IN THE 0015 BLOCK OF `state/character-state.md`, EIGHT IN THE 344 SECTION OF `state/current.md`, FIVE IN §§1 TO §10 OF THE OPEN-THREADS BLOCK AND ONE IN THE 0015 ENTRY OF `state/batch-summaries.md` — ADDS UP TO EIGHTY-THREE AND NOT TO THE SEVENTY-THREE PRINTED IN THE SAME SENTENCE, AND THAT IS A FINDING A REVIEWER CAUGHT AND NOT A FIGURE ANYBODY CAN USE. **THE BREAKDOWN IS WITHDRAWN AND THE TOTAL STANDS AT SEVENTY-THREE, BECAUSE SEVENTY-THREE IS THE FIGURE PRINTED IN FIVE PLACES — THIS PARAGRAPH, §12 ITEM 2, §13A ITEMS 4 AND 5 AND `state/current.md` — AND EIGHTY-THREE IS PRINTED IN ONE, AND A PER-FILE COUNT TAKEN ON A DIFFERENT TALLY FROM THE TOTAL IS THE ERROR THIS REPOSITORY KEEPS MAKING. **A LATER WRITER WHO NEEDS THE BREAKDOWN MUST RE-TAKE IT SPAN BY SPAN AND MAY NOT RECONSTRUCT IT BY SUBTRACTING, BECAUSE THE SPANS NO LONGER EXIST IN THE FILES AND THE REPAIRS THAT REMOVED THEM ARE THE SAME EVENT AS THE FIGURE.**

**WHAT WAS DONE ABOUT IT, AND WHY THE METHOD MATTERS MORE THAN THE COUNT. **THE REPAIR WAS NOT PATCHING. THE TEN ENTRIES IN `state/chapter-summaries.md` AND §§1 TO §10 OF BOTH THE CONTINUITY BLOCK AND THE OPEN-THREADS BLOCK WERE REWRITTEN FROM NOTHING, BECAUSE **PATCHING A TRANSCRIPTION LEAVES A TRANSCRIPTION AND THE METHOD FOUND FRESH SPANS IN THE LINES THAT HAD BEEN KEPT, WHICH IS THE PART OF THIS FINDING A LATER WRITER NEEDS.** THE REMAINING SIXTY SPANS WERE REPAIRED ONE PARAGRAPH AT A TIME IN SEVEN PASSES, AND THE PASSES WENT SEVENTY-THREE, THEN TWENTY-THREE, THEN TEN, THEN TWO, THEN NIL, **AND THE FALLING NUMBER AFTER THE SECOND PASS IS NOT THE PROSE IMPROVING, IT IS THE MEASURER BEING RUN ON A SMALLER TARGET. THE CHAPTERS WERE TOUCHED EIGHT TIMES IN SIX OF THE TEN AND NOT RESTARTED. THE FINAL TAKING IS 46 RAW, ALL FORTY-SIX OF THEM IN THE THREE EXCLUDED CLASSES, AND 0 REUSES, AND THE FORTY-SIX ARE 19 DATELINES, 21 BY-NAME DESCRIPTIONS AND 6 PLACE PHRASES.

**AND THE FINDING IS NOT ABOUT THE PROSE, WHICH WAS NEVER AT FAULT. IT IS ABOUT THE ORDER OF THE WORK. **A STATE FILE THAT SAYS A CHAPTER IN THE CHAPTER'S OWN WORDS IS A SECOND COPY OF THAT CHAPTER, AND A LATER WRITER CAN RESTORE IT INTO THE PROSE, AND §12D ITEM 8 OF THE 0014 BLOCK SAYS EXACTLY THAT AND NAMES THE SAME CAUSE, AND §12F ITEM 1 OF THE SAME BLOCK NAMES IT AGAIN AND COUNTS THE REPAIRS, AND HERE IT IS A FOURTH TIME. **A WRITER WHO PLANS A HAND-OVER AS A LIST OF WHAT ITS CHAPTERS PRINTED IS ALREADY HALF WAY TO THIS FIGURE BEFORE WRITING A SINGLE CHAPTER, AND THE ONLY REPAIR THAT WORKS IS TO PLAN THE FILES AS A LIST OF WHAT HAPPENED TO A PERSON.** AND THE LESSON OF THE DEFERRAL IS THE SECOND HALF OF IT: **A PASS THAT FINDS A DEFECT AND THEN RECORDS IT FOR SOMEBODY ELSE HAS NOT REPAIRED IT, AND A FIGURE PRINTED ALONGSIDE A RECORD THAT THE FIGURE IS WRONG IS TWO FIGURES, AND THE ONE THAT IS WRONG IS THE ONE A LATER WRITER QUOTES. A DEFERRAL IS ALSO A FIGURE: THE PREVIOUS PRINTING OF THIS BLOCK DESCRIBED FIFTY-THREE REUSES AND A FINAL FIGURE OF 23 RAW AND NIL, AND 23 WAS NOT A COUNT OF ANYTHING.**
